title: 微信 iLink 渠道
summary: `weixin` 与旧微信渠道的选型对照、扫码接入步骤、必填与可选配置、媒体与收信排查、迁移步骤。
text: 微信 iLink 渠道 weixin 与旧微信渠道的选型对照、扫码接入步骤、必填与可选配置、媒体与收信排查、迁移步骤。 # 微信 iLink 渠道 weixin 是独立渠道，与 wechat、wechatmp 不是同一套参数，接入前先按场景选渠道。 渠道选择 | 场景 | 选哪个 | | --- | --- | | 企业微信应用回调 | wechat（旧） | | 微信公众号回调 | wechatmp（旧） | | iLink 协议的微信能力 | weixin（新） | 新旧的主要区别： 入站方式：weixin 用长轮询拉取更新，旧版用 Webhook 回调。 回复要求：weixin 回复时必须带上本次会话的上下文标识，旧版不依赖。 登录方式：weixin 扫码拿机器人令牌，旧版用传统的企业 / 公众号参数。 媒体：weixin 走 CDN，加解密自己处理，旧版走平台原生接口。 状态：新接入用 weixin，旧版处于维护 / 兼容存量。 扫码接入 在渠道设置里选 weixin 后： 1. 点“生成二维码”； 2. 用微信扫码； 3. 点“等待确认”； 4. 系统自动回填机器人令牌、机器人 ID、用户 ID 和接口地址； 5. 保存账号配置。 回填成功后必须保存，长轮询才会真正生效。二维码有有效期，过期要重新生成。 设置与排查 必填三项：接口地址、机器人令牌、机器人 ID；再打开长连接开关。 可选增强：CDN 地址、机器人类型、允许的来话范围、轮询与接口超时、连续失败后的退避、路由标记。 媒体链路排查顺序：是否开了媒体、CDN 地址是否可达、解密密钥是否正确、附件是否超出大小限制。 回复报“缺少会话上下文标识”：这次回复没拿到上一条入站消息的会话标识。确认回复走的是同一会话，且入站消息里保留了它。 长时间收不到消息：依次看账号是否处于活跃状态、长连接是否开启、令牌和机器人 ID 是否有效、舰桥运行态里会话是否已过期。 会话频繁过期：一般是登录态失效，重新扫码拿新令牌并保存即可。 迁移步骤 1. 先并行运行：保留旧渠道，新流量优先走 weixin； 2. 按账号分批切换； 3. 盯住入站成功率、出站成功率、首包时延和失败排行； 4. 稳定后再把旧渠道标为维护态。 微信 iLink 渠道 渠道选择 扫码接入 设置与排查 迁移步骤

title: 聊天 WebSocket
summary: `/wunder/chat/ws` 的握手流程、客户端消息类型、服务端返回与断线重连方式。
text: 聊天 WebSocket /wunder/chat/ws 的握手流程、客户端消息类型、服务端返回与断线重连方式。 # 聊天 WebSocket /wunder/chat/ws 既是事件推送通道，也是会话的控制通道：启动执行、断线续传、观察、取消、回传审批都在同一条连接上完成。聊天与桌面实时会话都用它，没有 SSE 兜底。 适用场景 聊天工作台与桌面会话； 在同一条连接里启动、续传、观察、取消一次执行； 长连接保活与一致的实时状态。 握手流程 1. 创建会话，拿到会话 ID； 2. 建立 WebSocket 连接； 3. 发送 connect 握手； 4. 收到 ready； 5. 发送 start 启动执行； 6. 持续消费 event，直到收到本轮终态 turnterminal。 握手示例： 启动一次执行： 消息类型 客户端发往服务端： | kind | 作用 | | --- | --- | | connect | 握手与协议协商 | | start | 启动一次执行 | | resume | 断线后补齐落下的事件 | | watch | 只观察某个会话 | | cancel | 取消当前执行 | | approval | 回传审批决定 | | ping | 保活 | 服务端主要回 ready、event、error、pong。 设置与限制 需要消费的事件类别：排队中、审批已处理、出错、本轮结束。turnterminal 是单轮执行的终态信号，适合作为前端收敛条件。 start 必须显式带上会话 ID。 正文用 content，不是 /wunder 的 question。 resume（补事件）与 watch（看运行态）是两个不同动作。 这条连接上的审批只处理来自 WebSocket 的审批项。 断线与重连 不要退回 SSE。重新连上 /wunder/chat/ws，再按场景发送： resume：带上最后处理到的事件位置，补齐断线期间的事件； watch：重新观察当前会话的运行态。 聊天 WebSocket 适用场景 握手流程 消息类型 设置与限制 断线与重连

title: MCP 入口
summary: 对外暴露的 MCP 服务地址与内置的 `excute` / `doc2md` 两个工具，以及接入外部 MCP 服务的配置方式。
text: MCP 入口 对外暴露的 MCP 服务地址与内置的 excute / doc2md 两个工具，以及接入外部 MCP 服务的配置方式。 # MCP 入口 wunder 既能把自己暴露为 MCP 服务，也能作为 MCP 客户端接入外部服务。两个方向的入口与配置互不相同。 两个方向 | 方向 | 用途 | | --- | --- | | 对外暴露 | 让外部系统用 MCP 协议调用 wunder 的能力 | | 接入外部 | 把外部能力接进来给模型使用 | 对外暴露 对外入口是一个地址，走 Streamable HTTP。 接通顺序： 1. 外部系统按 MCP 协议连上这个地址； 2. wunder 自动完成协议版本协商，与旧服务互通时按双方都支持的范围协商，不用手写初始化步骤； 3. 调用具体工具。 目前内置对外提供两个工具：excute（执行）和 doc2md（文档转 Markdown）。工具名就是 excute，照这个名字调用。 接入外部服务 在配置里声明要接的 MCP 服务，给它名字、地址和传输方式，然后打开开关。启用后 wunder 把它当成一个可调用的服务。外部服务同样用 Streamable HTTP；服务是 Python 写的时按 Python 侧的协议版本协商，不一定具备最新的全部能力。 文档里常提到的外部服务通常承载数据库查询、数据库导出、知识库查询这类工具。 设置与限制 接入顺序：先在配置里声明服务 → 在舰桥确认工具清单能拉到 → 再开放给模型使用。 舰桥里有 MCP 的配置和调试入口，可以刷新工具清单、直接调远端工具验证。 MCP 工具不是旁路：它与内置工具、A2A 工具、技能、知识库工具、自建工具汇总进同一个工具视图。对模型来说，MCP 只是工具目录的一部分。 MCP 入口 两个方向 对外暴露 接入外部服务 设置与限制

title: wunder
summary: The four forms of wunder, its capability range, parallel tasks and the session queue, plus navigation entries into the manual.
headings: Concurrent Tasks and the Session Queue
text: wunder The four forms of wunder, its capability range, parallel tasks and the session queue, plus navigation entries into the manual. # wunder An agent orchestration platform Give it a goal, and the agent breaks the task down on its own, calls tools, and hands the results back. Forms The four forms are built on the same engine: | Form | Positioning | Who it's for | | --- | --- | --- | | Pupa | Local AI workbench, installed on your own computer | Individual users (the default entry point) | | Beehive | Cloud AI workbench, opened in a browser | Team members after the Hull is deployed | | Helm | Manual local entry point, used in a terminal | Command-line users / automation scripts | | Hull | User and agent management platform, shared by a team | Administrators | See the form matrix for the full comparison of tech stack, run model and OS support. The Pupa and the Helm don't depend on the Hull and can be installed and run on their own. The Bridge is the management interface that ships with the Hull, starts alongside it, and is aimed at administrators. Deploy the rest as needed: the Hull (server) covers shared use, permission management, channel access, and unified publishing — see Hull deployment; the Beehive (web) ships with the Hull, and members open it in a browser once it is deployed; the Helm (cli) covers terminal and automation scenarios — see Using the Helm. Default Entry Point Individual users start with the Pupa: download and install, and it opens as a local AI workbench. See Quick Start and Pupa quick start for the details. Capability Range Files and code: read, edit, run commands, refactor projects Office automation: organize documents, generate reports, process spreadsheets, take meeting notes Parallel subtasks: when several lines of work need to move at once, the main agent spins up a few subagents to work in parallel, then merges their results as they come back Scheduled tasks: periodic checks, recurring reminders, cross-channel message handling External service connections: turn common flows into skills Device interconnection: once a local device joins the cloud, the cloud can issue commands to the local node with your approval Concurrent Tasks and the Session Queue One agent can carry several independent task threads at the same time, without interfering with each other. You can also have several workspaces: a local directory, a cloud workspace, and a remote device workspace reached through device interconnection, distinguished by name in the interface. Sending a message mid-run won't bounce back: the session queue is on by default, so new messages wait in the queue instead of hitting a "user busy" error. Interfaces Pupa interface: the main window has two pages, "Chat" and "Settings"; everything else appears as panels and dialogs Beehive interface: a single-page app in the browser Bridge interface: the administrator's governance and debugging backend Interface Overview: how the four forms compare Navigation First time → Quick Start Download and install → Pupa quick start Interface map → Interface Overview Understand the system in depth → Core Concepts Documentation hub → Documentation Hub Doc ecosystem navigation → Common Docs Directory First launch fails or something goes wrong → Troubleshooting or FAQ wunder Forms Default Entry Point Capability Range Concurrent Tasks and the Session Queue Interfaces Navigation

title: Quick Start
summary: Install and model configuration, the first message, how user turns and model turns are presented, plus the checks for a working setup and where to look after a failure.
headings: Where to look after a failure
text: Quick Start Install and model configuration, the first message, how user turns and model turns are presented, plus the checks for a working setup and where to look after a failure. # Quick Start Individual users start with the Pupa (desktop) — download the installer and it runs; there is no Hull (server) to deploy first. The four sections below follow install, model configuration, your first message, and the run itself. Download and install Download the installer matching your system from Releases. The Pupa targets 32-bit Win7 and Ubuntu 18.04 and also covers modern Windows / Linux. Install or extract it, then launch. In a development environment you can also run the launch script directly (on Windows that's run.bat, or run wunder-frontend-slint straight). It calls the engine natively in-process — it takes no local port and needs no local HTTP/WebSocket relay. Configure the model Open "Settings → Model" and fill in your API Key and endpoint URL (in the form https://example.com/v1); verify once with "Test connection" before saving. Fill in the model name and parameters per your provider's guidance. Data stays on your machine: local SQLite by default, with the configuration directory at /.wunder; model requests go to the remote endpoint you configured. Send your first message Back on the chat page, type: and press Enter to send. The run A run is shown by user turn / model turn: User turn = counted once for each message you send Model turn = one model call in the engine's main loop (which may include a batch of tool calls); tool calls don't count as a separate model turn When the timeline shows tool batches, a "work process" entry for each turn, and a final reply, the run is finished. Capabilities available locally Local first: data stays on your machine and can work offline; the network is used only to reach models and web pages Desktop control: a desktop controller and desktop monitor (requires a vision model) Interactive terminal: winpty-based on Windows, PTY-based on Linux Screenshot capture, voice input, tray, system notifications, and global hotkeys One agent can have several independent task threads at once, and workspaces can be multiple too (local + cloud + remote device workspaces reached through device interlink) Edit the agent directly: change the system prompt, approval mode, and tool set at any time Checks for a working setup You can start a conversation successfully You can see the intermediate steps and tool-call batches You can get the final result and copy it When you scroll up to review history, new output doesn't yank you back to the bottom When something fails, you know which page to check Where to look after a failure | Symptom | Check first | | --- | --- | | Launch screen never finishes | First-run troubleshooting | | Model request 401/403 | Settings → Model → Test connection; Configuration reference | | Message during a run rejected as "user busy" | Whether the session queue was turned off | | Interface stutters, messages don't refresh | Troubleshooting | Other forms The Hull, the Beehive, and the Helm are installed per scenario: The Hull (server): multi-user sharing, permission management, channel integration, and publishing and governing agent apps. See Hull deployment. The Beehive (web): the cloud AI workbench delivered with the Hull, accessed in a browser; its pages are delivered by a separate web-service container, on 18001 by default. See Beehive interface. The Helm (cli): the manual local entry point for terminals and automation. See Helm usage. Quick Start Download and install Configure the model Send your first message The run Capabilities available locally Checks for a working setup Where to look after a failure Other forms

title: Starting with the Pupa (Desktop)
summary: The local AI workbench: install and launch, layout of local data, the two-page main window, first-run configuration, capabilities unique to the desktop, and interaction constraints.
text: Starting with the Pupa (Desktop) The local AI workbench: install and launch, layout of local data, the two-page main window, first-run configuration, capabilities unique to the desktop, and interaction constraints. # Starting with the Pupa (Desktop) It calls the engine natively in-process, has no port of its own, and routes through no HTTP/WebSocket relay. Individual users install just this — there is no Hull (server) to deploy first. Prerequisites | Scenario | Choose the Pupa | | --- | --- | | Want to start right away, without deploying a service first | ✅ | | Need to work with local files, windows, and browsers | ✅ | | Prefer a graphical interface | ✅ | | Need an interactive terminal and screenshot capture | ✅ | | Need a tray, system notifications, and global hotkeys | ✅ | | May connect to a remote later, but want to get running now | ✅ | | Need multi-user governance and an admin backend | ❌ Choose the Hull (server) | | Need to access it in a browser | ❌ Choose the Beehive (web, ships with the Hull) | The Pupa covers single-user local scenarios; sharing among several people runs through the Hull and the Beehive. Install and launch Download the installer for your system from Releases. Executable: wunder-frontend-slint Development launch: on Windows, use the project's bundled run.bat Platforms: primarily targets 32-bit Win7 and Ubuntu 18.04; modern Windows / Linux also run No port, no required arguments: it calls the engine in-process right after launch There's also a compatibility bridge port (default 18123) that serves only legacy-compatible clients; day-to-day use doesn't go through it The Electron / Tauri frontend shells are no longer maintained day-to-day and get no new features (this doesn't mean the Pupa backend stops being maintained) Local data | Content | Location | | --- | --- | | Root directory | WUNDERHOME → /.wunder by default | | Workspace | /.wunder/workspace | | Temporary directory | WUNDERDESKTOPTEMPROOT | | Desktop settings | /config/desktop.settings.json | | Sessions and tool logs | local SQLite | To move to a new machine, copy /.wunder across. "Local first" means data stays on your machine; it doesn't affect reaching remote models or web pages. On startup it scans the work tree (up to 4096 items), restores the state of unfinished tasks from last time, and clears session locks and leftover tasks. Interface layout The main window has two switchable pages, Chat and Settings; everything else hangs off them as panels and dialogs. Chat page Left column: the task and thread tree, the working-directory area (local file tree + usage bar + cloud workspaces), and the settings entry at the bottom Right column: the top bar (workspace / thread name) + timeline + composer With no thread selected, a welcome page shows; file preview and online editing pop out as overlays without changing the two-column structure One agent can run several independent task threads in parallel, and workspaces can be multiple: local + cloud + remote device workspaces reached through device interlink Settings page 12 categories: General, Account, Model, Tools, Agents, Personas, Scheduled, Memory, Channels, Prompt packs, Archive, Help. The category navigation supports search filtering. There is no "device interlink" category. First run Launch preparation On launch, a lightweight splash screen appears first while local working directories, configuration, and sessions are prepared. The window appearing doesn't mean sessions are ready; you can start working once the workbench opens. First launches or slower devices may take longer to prepare. Model configuration Settings → Model → Add: API Key Endpoint URL (a neutral endpoint such as https://example.com/v1) Model name and parameters (temperature, context length, and so on) Confirm with "Test connection" before saving. This is also where you hook up TTS, image, and video models; TTS can currently only be configured — there is no playback implementation. Account profile Settings → Account: username, email, avatar; set a login password if you plan to use it long-term. First conversation Back on the chat page, type: When you see the model think → a batch of tools → the final reply landing in the chat area, you're up and running. Capabilities unique to the Pupa None of these exist on the Beehive, the Bridge, or the Helm: Interactive terminal (winpty on Windows, PTY on Linux) Screenshot capture (X11 on Linux, Win32 APIs on Windows) Tray and system notifications Global hotkeys Voice input Device interlink surfaces Only two interlink surfaces are available in the Pupa: 1. The cloud workspaces in the sidebar's working-directory area: when the network is unavailable they clearly show "offline" alongside a "connect" button 2. The remote command approval dialog: high-risk commands (L3) in device interlink pop up for confirmation with a red border, showing the command level, risk, and source, plus a "don't remember" hint The Settings page still holds a set of device-interlink options, but they aren't wired to any interface; that entry point is not open yet. Resetting the working state When sessions, subagents, or workspaces get into a bad state, use "Settings → General → Reset workspace state": It does: stop running sessions, clear queued tasks, clean up session locks It keeps: skills, knowledge bases, long-term memory, user configuration, workspace files, session history It clears working state; it is not a factory reset. Interaction constraints Two default behaviors are worth separating: The session queue is on by default: sending another message during a run queues it instead of rejecting it as "user busy." Turn it off and messages sent during a run are bounced outright without entering the queue bar. The subagent activity indicator: when a task has spawned subagents, the chat area shows the child runs that are still working; subagents are temporary work units the main agent creates, reclaimed once the task ends. Starting with the Pupa (Desktop) Prerequisites Install and launch Local data Interface layout Chat page Settings page First run Launch preparation Model configuration Account profile First conversation Capabilities unique to the Pupa Device interlink surfaces Resetting the working state Interaction constraints

title: Form matrix
summary: How the program forms compare on tech stack, purpose, run model and OS support, plus which form to pick for your scenario.
text: Form matrix How the program forms compare on tech stack, purpose, run model and OS support, plus which form to pick for your scenario. # Form matrix wunder is an agent scheduling platform. One engine is shipped as several program forms; the difference is only in the access layer. | Icon | Form | Tech stack | Purpose | Run model | OS support | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 🚀 | Hull server | Rust + axum 0.8; PostgreSQL | User and agent management platform (multi-tenancy, users and org units, agent app build and publish, gateway access and scheduling) | Long-running server process, Docker deployment, HTTP / WebSocket access | Linux / Docker | | 🐉 | Bridge web | Plain HTML + CSS + JavaScript (web/, no build step) | Hull's admin console (four panel groups: system, agents, debug, docs) | Browser access, statically mounted by Hull at / | Any browser | | 🐝 | Beehive web | Vue 3 + TypeScript (Vite build, frontend/) | Cloud AI workbench (Hull's user side) | Browser access; build output frontend/dist is served read-only by the nginx container (default port 18001) and is not hosted by Hull | Any browser | | 🍯 | Pupa desktop | Rust + Slint 1.18 (default frontend frontend-slint/, native UI, software rendering); SQLite | Local AI workbench (the flagship form, works out of the box) | Local desktop process, native in-process calls to the engine (no local network hop); Electron / Tauri shells are no longer maintained | Windows 7 x86 and up; Linux (ubuntu 18.04 baseline) x64 / arm64 AppImage | | ⚙ | Helm cli | Rust terminal TUI (ratatui + crossterm); SQLite | Manual local entry point (terminal, scriptable, automation) | Local terminal process, direct in-process engine calls, JSONL output supported | Windows 7 and up (GNU toolchain); Linux amd64 / arm64 (ubuntu 18.04 sysroot) | All forms share the same engine (wunder-runtime) and core (wunder-core): threads, tools, storage abstractions, realtime events and permission semantics are one body of code, and the difference is only in the access layer. Pupa and Helm do not depend on Hull and can be installed and run on their own. Choosing a form Individual users → Pupa (desktop). The local AI workbench, the default entry point for personal use, ready to run after install. Teams, or anyone working in a browser → Beehive (web). Hull's user side, provided with Hull; once Hull is deployed, members reach it in a browser. Terminal and scripting → Helm (cli). The manual local entry point, terminal-driven, scriptable, automation-friendly. Multi-user management and governance → Hull (server). Multi-tenancy, user and org-unit management, agent app build and publish, unified gateway access and scheduling. The admin console is the Bridge (web), which starts with Hull and is aimed at administrators. Form matrix Choosing a form

title: Core Concepts
summary: The Diverse, Fast, Superior, and Efficient cores, four design principles, four forms, deeper pages by topic, and capabilities that are removed or restricted.
text: Core Concepts The Diverse, Fast, Superior, and Efficient cores, four design principles, four forms, deeper pages by topic, and capabilities that are removed or restricted. wunder is an agent-scheduling platform: hand it a goal and the agent breaks the task down, calls tools, and delivers results. The feature list lives in Tools and the Capability Quick Reference. Diverse, Fast, Superior, Efficient Diversity and strength set the capability surface; speed and efficiency constrain how it is built: a thin access layer, a short execution path, and bounded queues, caches, views, and context. | Core | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Diverse | Multi-platform, multi-form. One core and engine support the Pupa, Beehive, Helm, and Hull across Windows 7 x86 and up, Linux (ubuntu18.04 baseline) x64 / arm64, Docker, and browsers; models, channels, and workspaces extend through the same access layer | | Fast | Fast startup, fast response. Local forms call the engine in-process without local HTTP; threads and history restore directly from local storage; streaming events are frame-coalesced and projected incrementally, and tools run in parallel where allowed | | Superior | Strong stability, high intelligence. Queues, caches, views, and context are bounded, with session locks, round caps, quotas, and retry circuit breaking for long runs; goal mode, subagents, the tool chain, long-term memory, and knowledge bases carry complex tasks from decomposition to delivery | | Efficient | Low CPU and memory use, low context consumption. A native Rust process with local SQLite needs no browser runtime; tool-result trimming, frozen prompts that reuse cache, one-time memory-index injection, and micro-compaction and history compaction keep token consumption down | The nine capabilities expanded page by page — goal, compatibility, context compression, subagents, scheduled tasks, channels, memory, multithreading, and multi-tenancy — live under Capabilities › Core Capabilities. Design Principles | Principle | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Everything revolves around the thread | The thread (= session) is the unit of execution, not "one Q&A". A single agent can hold several independent task threads at once, and scheduling, locks, and realtime state are all isolated per thread | | Everything is a tool | Everything the model can do is exposed through a unified tool interface; canonical names are mostly Chinese (读取文件, 执行命令, 记忆管理), and English aliases are normalized before routing | | One engine across forms | There is only one core and one engine; the four forms differ only at the access layer | | Boundaries and governance are built in | Prompt freezing, approval tiers, daily quotas, and bounded views with pagination are part of the skeleton, not left to the upper layers | Forms | Form | Role | | --- | --- | | Pupa (desktop) | A local AI workbench, the default entry for individuals; a local desktop process that calls the engine in-process, with a local SQLite | | Beehive (web) | A cloud AI workbench reached from a browser; no process of its own, using the Hull's storage | | Helm (cli) | A hands-on local entry driven from a terminal and easy to script; a local process with a local SQLite | | Hull (server) | The user- and agent-management platform: multi-tenancy, units, app build-and-release, and gateway access; a service process plus the engine, with the Bridge built in | The Pupa and the Helm do not depend on the Hull and can run and ship on their own. The Electron / Tauri front-end shells are no longer maintained day to day and are no longer described as a capability. Deeper Pages by Topic | Topic | Page | | --- | --- | | Which stages a message passes through | Architecture | | How sessions, threads, and rounds are numbered | Sessions and Rounds | | Realtime push and resuming after a disconnect | Streaming Execution | | Workspaces and file safety | Workspaces and Working Directory | | Status indicators | Runtime State | | Tool sources and governance | Tool System | | The four layers of prompts, skills, and capabilities | Prompts and Skills | | Memory shapes and troubleshooting | Long-term Memory | | Tokens and quotas | Tokens and Quotas | | Persistent goal mode | Goal Mode | | Animated companions | Companion System | | Anomaly and truncation behavior | Boundary Handling | | How a thread advances round by round | Agent Loop | | The four layers of capabilities | Tools | | The process is visible and a disconnect can resume | Realtime | | Bounded views, budgets, and circuit breaking | Stability | | Logs, metrics, and thread trajectories | Observability | Reading Paths First time on the Pupa: Quickstart → Agent Loop → Tools → Memory → Context Compression. Administrator / governance: Multi-user Management → Stability → Observability → Channels → Configuration Reference. Integration and development: Architecture → Chat WebSocket → Streaming Execution. Limits "Several agents can form a swarm and collaborate" — they cannot. The only collaborative form is the subagent: a temporary work unit the main agent creates and reclaims when the task ends. Swarm orchestration (swarm tools, hives, orchestration mode, team runs, swarm packs) has been removed from the engine and the scheduling surface; a few terminal strings and UI labels still carry the old wording, but that is leftover to clean up, not a capability. "Every listed tool is usable" — it is not. The default usable set is a fixed tier, and 网页搜索 and ptc are currently temporarily withdrawn (code kept, invisible to model and user), not deleted. "Editing the prompt affects the current conversation at once" — it does not. Once a thread first fixes its system prompt, it is frozen. "What the UI shows is the back-end truth" — the UI consumes a bounded view (pagination plus a byte budget), not the full history. When the content looks wrong, trust the thread ledger. "Stopping maintenance of the front-end shell stops the Pupa back end" — they are two different things. The Pupa runs the local native UI with in-process native calls by default, and its execution, tools, and storage semantics still reuse the engine. title: Deploying the Hull (Server)
summary: An optional form. Multi-tenancy governance, channel integration and agent-app publishing; the Bridge on 18000 and the Beehive delivered on 18001, plus Compose and cargo startup, first login and the post-deployment checklist.
text: Deploying the Hull (Server) An optional form. Multi-tenancy governance, channel integration and agent-app publishing; the Bridge on 18000 and the Beehive delivered on 18001, plus Compose and cargo startup, first login and the post-deployment checklist. # Deploying the Hull (Server) The Hull (server) is the user-and-agent management platform and an optional form. The Pupa (desktop) is enough for personal use; deploy the Hull only when you need multi-tenancy, user and organization management, channel integration, building and publishing agent apps, and unified gateway scheduling. Port layout Once deployed, the Hull provides three access entries at once (default ports, all overridable by environment variables): | Interface | Carrier | Default port | | --- | --- | --- | | Hull API | The Hull service itself | 18000 (overridable with WUNDERHOST / WUNDERPORT) | | Bridge | The Hull's built-in native admin pages, no build needed | The same port as the Hull, 18000 | | Beehive | A standalone frontend app, built and delivered by the web-service container | A separate container, 18001 (overridable with NGINXPORT) | Note: the Beehive is not hosted by the Hull. The Hull process only serves the Bridge pages and directories such as avatars and ppt; the Beehive is delivered by a standalone web-service container on 18001. Other related service ports: sandbox mode 9001, onlyoffice 18080, drawio 18081, PostgreSQL 5432, extra-mcp 18004. Prerequisites | Scenario | Choose the Hull | | --- | --- | | Several people sharing one system | ✅ | | Need an admin backend (the Bridge) | ✅ | | Need to connect channels such as Feishu, WeCom, and QQ Bot | ✅ | | Need unified governance, auditing, and quotas | ✅ | | Need to build and publish agent apps | ✅ | | Just personal use | ❌ Choose the Pupa (desktop) | Before deploying Docker and Docker Compose (recommended) At least 4 GB of available memory PostgreSQL (built into the compose setup; a single machine can also switch to SQLite) Time zone: Asia/Shanghai by default in the compose setup Docker Compose deployment This starts the Hull service (18000 by default), the sandbox (9001, with /health), onlyoffice (18080), drawio (18081), extra-mcp, PostgreSQL (5432), the Beehive frontend build container, and the web-service container (18001). Running locally (cargo) Configuration load order: first the file named by WUNDERCONFIGPATH, else config/wunder.yaml; ${ENV} placeholders in the YAML are expanded; environment variables have the highest priority and take effect last; missing fields are filled in from the example template. Note: the Rust process does not load .env — .env is only consumed by the compose and script layers; set real environment variables for the Hull process itself. Known issue: starting directly with config/wunder-example.yaml fails to parse and silently falls back to the default configuration — point explicitly at config/wunder.yaml, or name it with WUNDERCONFIGPATH. Access entries | Entry | Address | | --- | --- | | Bridge (admin interface) | http:// :18000/ | | API | http:// :18000/wunder/ | | Beehive (user interface) | http:// :18001/ | | MCP server | http:// :18000/wunder/mcp | | External workflows | http:// :18000/wunder/external/workflow | | Health check | GET http:// :18000/wunder/i18n | First login The admin credentials are in config/wunder.yaml; change the admin password immediately after first login. Passwords are stored with Argon2 encryption; login tokens are opaque random strings (in the form wund , wundr , wundc , not JWTs); refresh tokens rotate by family, and replaying the same refresh token revokes the whole family. Post-deployment checklist 1. Change the admin password 2. Bridge → Model configuration: add LLM / TTS / image / video model endpoints and API keys 3. Bridge → Organization management: confirm the organization tree (up to 4 levels deep), importing config/orgunits.json if needed 4. Bridge → Preset agents: create preset agent card templates that declare which fields users may customize 5. Bridge → User management: add users or open self-service registration 6. For channel integration: Feishu / WeCom / WeChat / QQ Bot / WhatsApp Cloud / weixin / xmpp (7 provided by default) 7. Watch health: the Bridge's "internal status" page, and the /wunder/admin/monitor interface Multi-tenancy and governance Users and organizations managed in layers; permissions assigned by role (admin / leader / user), with data isolated by user and agent Online status shown in three columns: Beehive / Pupa / Helm User levels and quotas (up to 200 levels) Channel integration 7 registered by default: WhatsApp Cloud / Feishu / QQ Bot / WeChat / WeChat Official Account / weixin / xmpp Of these, Feishu / QQ Bot / xmpp / weixin use long-lived connections; the rest use webhooks only Telegram / Discord / Slack / LINE / DingTalk are not supported; they exist only as generic webhook entries in the directory Inbound queue capacity 512, concurrency 8, enqueue timeout 80ms; outbound messages are persisted and retried with exponential backoff Observability Logs go to both the console and a JSONL file (rolled daily), written to ./config/data/logs/server by default, at info level by default, and never cleaned up by default (retention 0) Runtime metrics: blocking, queueing, long tasks, and loop cadence, plus alerts and thresholds Channel run logs: the most recent 300 entries kept in memory, with duplicate floods within 20 seconds deduplicated Security and isolation Read / write / execute tools in the cloud all run inside the sandbox; with no available sandbox endpoint they fail outright and do not fall back to the host. One container per user, mounting only that user's directory, with tenant isolation handled by the sandbox. Exec policy has three states: allow / audit / enforce Approval modes: suggest / autoedit / fullauto, with fullauto the default High-risk command list: rm, rm -rf, mkfs, dd, chmod 777 Sandbox container resources: 8 CPU cores, 8096MB memory, 256 processes, 300s timeout Configuration files The config/ directory holds the engine's main wunder.yaml, an example configuration, sandbox runtime configuration, MCP configuration, organization units, i18n copy, version numbers, and font and drawing configuration, among others; there are also the benchmark/, data/, fonts/, ppttemplates/, presetworkercards/, prompts/, and skills/ subdirectories. Configuration supports hot reloading at runtime, and changes are written straight back to the YAML file. title: Using the Helm (CLI)
summary: The manual local entry point. An interactive session on a TTY and a one-shot run off it; 11 subcommands, the full set of 22 slash commands, an exec --json event stream, and the complete cloud subcommand family; scheduled tasks and engine queueing are off on the Helm.
headings: Capability differences from the other interfaces
text: Using the Helm (CLI) The manual local entry point. An interactive session on a TTY and a one-shot run off it; 11 subcommands, the full set of 22 slash commands, an exec --json event stream, and the complete cloud subcommand family; scheduled tasks and engine queueing are off on the Helm. # Using the Helm (CLI) The manual local entry point, an optional form. For daily use, install the Pupa (desktop); reach for the Helm when you work terminal-driven, scripted, or automated. It calls the engine in-process, reusing the same configuration, tools, and storage rather than standing up a separate execution path. Prerequisites | Scenario | Choose the Helm | | --- | --- | | Prefer working in a terminal | ✅ | | Need scripting, automation, CI/CD | ✅ | | Need piped output (JSONL) | ✅ | | Need the cloud subcommands to operate device interlink | ✅ | | Don't want to install the Pupa | ✅ | | Need a graphical interface | ❌ Choose the Pupa | | Need browser access | ❌ Choose the Beehive (ships with the Hull) | Install and launch TTY (stdin/stdout/stderr are all TTYs): opens the interactive session — a ratatui TUI rendered with an inline viewport (Viewport::Inline), so your shell scrollback is preserved Non-TTY: degrades to a one-shot run; pipelines and scripts take this path Data directory: WUNDERHOME → /.wunder User configuration: /.wunder/config.toml Your first session: Seeing the model think → a batch of tools → results → a reply means it's working. wunder-cli doctor checks whether the local runtime environment is ready. Subcommands | Subcommand | Alias | Action | | --- | --- | --- | | exec | e | Run a single agent task non-interactively; --json produces a JSONL event stream | | resume | — | Resume a previous session | | trajectory | — | Inspect, search, and export thread trajectories; JSON and bidirectional cursors | | tool | — | Run built-in, MCP, or skill tools directly | | mcp | — | Manage local MCP servers | | skills | — | Manage the current user's local skills | | config | — | View and change runtime configuration | | stress-thread | — | Generate local synthetic threads for rendering stress tests | | doctor | — | Diagnose the local runtime environment | | cloud | — | Manage the local cloud connection and device interlink | | completion | — | Generate shell completion scripts | The cloud subcommands The full set for device interlink and cloud workspace operations: The exec --json event stream One JSON object per line, with event names thread / turn / item.. For pipelines and automation: Slash commands 22 in total: | Command | Alias | Action | | --- | --- | --- | | /help | /h | Help | | /status | — | Current status | | /resume | /r | Resume a previous session | | /trajectory | /trace | Inspect the current or specified thread trajectory | | /new | — | New thread | | /clear | /cls | Clear the screen | | /model | — | Switch model; /model add registers an endpoint | | /permissions | /perm / /approvals / /approval | Permissions and approvals | | /plan | — | Plan panel | | /goal | — | Goal-state management | | /edit | — | Edit | | /init | — | Initialize | | /attach | — | Attachments | | /diff | — | Patch diff | | /review | — | Review | | /skills | — | Skill list | | /rename | — | Rename | | /compact | — | Compress the conversation | | /mcp | — | MCP management | | /config | /config show is a sub-form | Show the effective config; /config edit opens config.toml | | /exit | — | Exit | | /quit | /q | Exit | There are no cloud, cron, channel, memory, or knowledge slash commands: cloud is a subcommand, and the other four have no management interface on the Helm. Trajectory logs Run /trajectory (alias /trace) in the interactive session to inspect the current thread, or /trajectory for another thread. In the task center, press t to inspect the selected thread without switching the executing thread. The viewer provides sequence / elapsed-time controls, turn and tool-group folding, zoom, three input/model/tool lanes, a ledger, and item details. Wide terminals show details beside the ledger; press i for a separate detail page on narrow terminals. | Key | Trajectory action | | --- | --- | | ↑↓ / j k, PageUp PageDown | Select records; automatically read older / newer records at window edges | | Enter | Inspect the selected user turn; inside a turn, toggle detail focus | | i / → | Toggle detail focus; arrows and page keys scroll focused details | | Tab / Shift+Tab | Cycle applicable overview, preview, raw, params, result, schema, and timing tabs | | h / l in details | Pan long lines horizontally | | d, + -, 0 | Sequence / elapsed time, zoom around selection, reset zoom | | t, Space, c | Fold all turns, selected turn, or tools in a model round | | / | Enter a full-text query; up to 20 hits per request, refine if more are available | | f, r | Toggle live follow, refresh / retry; manual browsing pauses follow | | y, e | Copy the current detail tab, export full JSONL to the launch directory | | Esc / q, ? | Return one level, show help | The viewer uses shared engine projections and body reads in the background. It retains a maximum of 600 ledger rows, with bidirectional cursors to reread evicted records. Detail previews are limited to 1 MiB and 16,384 lines per tab with an explicit notice; export retrieves the full log. Exports retain user-visible records; system prompt contents remain hidden. For scripts and pipelines, use the subcommand. Without a thread ID it selects the most recent thread in the current workspace: Use returned nextbefore / nextafter cursors; --before and --after are mutually exclusive. --raw or global --json emits structured data. Export destinations must not already exist. A final exportcomplete record distinguishes a complete export from an interrupted file. Keys | Key | Action | | --- | --- | | / | Open the command palette | | Enter | Send | | ! | Run shell directly | | Shift+Enter / Ctrl+J | New line | | Tab | Complete | | @ | File mention | | # | Skill mention | | $ | Tool mention | | Ctrl+V | Paste an image | | Drag in an image or file | Attach | | Alt+, / Alt+. | Lower / raise reasoning effort | | Ctrl+R / Ctrl+S | Search input history | | Ctrl+G | External editor | | Ctrl+O | Copy the last reply | | Ctrl+T | Full transcript | | Ctrl+L | Clear the screen and start a new session | | Ctrl+C | Exit | | Esc | Interrupt the current turn; clear the draft when idle; close the shortcut panel | | F3 | View output and select a card | | Enter (in the F3 panel) | Expand / collapse | | F2 | Run reminders | | Mouse click | Select a card; click its Show details / Show less row to fold or unfold; click in the composer to place the caret | | Mouse drag / double click / triple click | Drag copies the marked rows, a double click takes the word under the pointer, a triple click the whole line; right click re-copies whatever is still marked | | Ctrl + click a link | Open that http/https/file href with the system's default program | | F4 | Toggle mouse mode: capture (app handles clicks and the wheel) ↔ native (the terminal keeps selection, copy and its own wheel) | | ? | Shortcut panel | | ← | Task center | Capability differences from the other interfaces Only the Helm has these The exec --json event-stream scripting contract The full set of cloud subcommands doctor local runtime diagnostics stress-thread local synthetic threads completion shell completions tool / mcp / skills run straight from the command line (without going through the agent main loop) The Helm lacks these Scheduled tasks are explicitly off: you can't add, modify, enable, or immediately run a scheduled task; viewing status, listing, deleting, and disabling still work — so you'll see old task lists, but the Helm won't schedule anything new. Engine queueing is explicitly off too: sending another message during a run doesn't join a queue; it hits the session lock outright and is judged "this user already has a running session," returning only once the busy window elapses. This is the opposite of the Pupa, which forces the queue open. To interject, queue, or rewrite the next message during a run, use the Pupa or the Beehive. Channels, knowledge bases, long-term memory, and personas have no management interface on the Helm No voice input: the Helm has no ASR; paste images with Ctrl+V or drag-and-drop No interactive terminal UI: the host is itself the terminal; shell access goes through the ! prefix No screenshot capture, tray, or global hotkeys Runtime files By default the Helm keeps runtime files under /.wunder: Runtime configuration and SQLite state: /.wunder/cli/WUNDERTEMP/ Engine configuration YAML: /.wunder/config/wunder.yaml, the same file the Pupa uses; the Helm reads it back, projects its own layers onto it and writes it out, so the model list is visible to both User tools and skills: /.wunder/usertools/ and /.wunder/skills/ Temporary-file API: WUNDERTEMPDIRROOT points to the same /.wunder/cli/WUNDERTEMP/ When a script needs an isolated runtime directory, override it with --temp-root . Automation scenarios Calling exec --json in CI/CD pipelines to consume JSONL Batch tasks: an external scheduler looping over exec Pipelines: cat input.txt | wunder-cli triggers the non-TTY degradation Combining with tool / mcp / skills for pure tool runs Scheduled tasks don't belong on the Helm: it turns cron off; put them on the Pupa or Beehive scheduled-tasks page Using the Helm (CLI) Prerequisites Install and launch Subcommands The cloud subcommands The exec --json event stream Slash commands Trajectory logs Keys Capability differences from the other interfaces Only the Helm has these The Helm lacks these Runtime files Automation scenarios

title: Documentation Directory
summary: A guide to the repo's documentation ecosystem: how the overview and design docs, technical manual, API reference, user manual, performance standards and scoring, changelog, and lessons-learned divide the work, and how to read them.
text: Documentation Directory A guide to the repo's documentation ecosystem: how the overview and design docs, technical manual, API reference, user manual, performance standards and scoring, changelog, and lessons-learned divide the work, and how to read them. # Documentation Directory wunder's documentation falls into seven categories, each answering a different kind of question. When writing docs, don't mix them: design docs cover boundaries and rationale, the technical manual covers engineering execution (change points, run method, verification points), the API reference covers interface contracts, the user manual covers user and admin operations, performance standards and scoring cover conventions and quantification, the changelog covers the flow of changes, and lessons-learned covers recurring problems. Documentation categories | Category | Location | Audience | When to look | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Overview design | docs/总体设计.md, docs/wunder系统简介.md | All readers | To grasp the product positioning and the division between forms in one line | | Design docs | docs/设计文档/ (01–13 plus topical pieces on context compression / real-time sync / tools / the memory system / the goal-state system) | Architecture reviews, trade-off decisions | To learn why it's designed this way and where the boundaries are | | Technical manual | docs/技术说明书/ (chapters 01–13 + README) | Engineering executors | To learn change points, run method, verification points | | API reference | docs/API文档.md | Interface consumers | Concrete HTTP / WebSocket endpoint contracts | | User manual | docs/使用说明书/zh-CN/, docs/使用说明书/en/ | Users and admins | Interface maps and steps for concrete operations | | Performance standards and scoring | docs/性能标准.md, docs/性能评分体系.md, docs/性能基线/ | Operations and benchmark testers | Before/after comparison, pass/fail judgment, per-form independent scoring | | Changelog / lessons-learned | docs/功能迭代.md, docs/经验教训.md | Project maintainers | The change flow each round; recurring pitfalls | The user manual (this site) docs/使用说明书/site.json drives the navigation for both the Chinese and English sites. The Chinese site is the authoritative version; the English site follows it. Start | Page | Content | | --- | --- | | Quick Start | Get your first task running in 4 steps | | Pupa intro | Individual users download and go | | Hull deployment | Multi-user sharing, unified management | | Helm usage | Terminal-driven, automation | | First-run troubleshooting | Locate install / launch / access failures by form | | Manual overview | Navigation home | | Documentation directory | This page | Surfaces | Page | Content | | --- | --- | | Surfaces overview | The four forms' division and capability matrix | | Pupa interface | The main window's two pages + settings' 12 categories | | Beehive interface | The single-page app in the browser | | Bridge interface | The admin governance backend | Other sections Tools → /docs/en/tools/ Capabilities → /docs/en/capabilities/ Help → /docs/en/help/ Design docs (docs/设计文档/) They answer "why it's designed this way" and don't cover how to change things. Numbers 01–13 form the backbone: | Number | Topic | | --- | --- | | 01 | System overall design | | 02 | Agent core design | | 03 | Real-time projection system design | | 05 | Tools, skills, and MCP system design | | 06 | Memory, knowledge, and workspace system design | | 07 | Integration, gateway, and channel system design | | 08 | Data storage and state-model design | | 09 | User-side frontend design | | 10 | Admin-side and operations backend design | | 11 | Desktop-CLI local form design | | 12 | Security, permissions, and isolation design | | 13 | Observability, testing, and acceptance design | Topical sub-pages: context compression design, real-time sync design, tool design, memory system design, goal-state system design, and the apply-patch tool refactor plan; there's also a Beehive high-volume thread-log rendering optimization plan (at the root of docs/, the plan rewritten and the implementation still to be done). Technical manual (docs/技术说明书/) They answer "change points, run method, verification points" and don't cover boundaries and rationale. Chapters 01–13: | Number | Topic | | --- | --- | | 01 | System overview and terminology | | 02 | Repository structure and module responsibilities | | 03 | Runtime and execution path | | 04 | Real-time projection and communication path | | 05 | Tools, skills, MCP, and external capabilities | | 06 | Data storage, workspaces, and configuration | | 07 | Interfaces, gateway, and channel integration | | 08 | Deployment, startup, and run modes | | 09 | Development, extension, and change flow | | 10 | Operations, troubleshooting, and acceptance | | 11 | Tool-result trimming and the observability path | | 12 | The persona system | | 13 | The goal-state system | Extra: Docker acceptance for throughput tests. API reference (docs/API文档.md) A single file, from the interface consumer's perspective. All HTTP endpoints use the /wunder/ prefix (not /api/); error responses write back x-trace-id and x-error-code response headers. WebSocket channels include chat/ws, ws, gateway/ws, interlink/ws, interlink/remotews, userworld/ws, and desktop/lan/ws (event names are scattered rather than centrally enumerated). Performance standards and scoring (docs/) | Document | Content | | --- | --- | | docs/性能标准.md | Same-environment, same-entry before/after comparison + standard-entry table | | docs/性能评分体系.md | Three forms scored independently 0–100 and weighted; not summable across forms | | docs/性能基线/ | Historical baseline snapshots; the latest include 2026-10-13-server-capacity.md and 2026-10-13-thread-view-v3.md | Conventions: performance isn't an adjective. Any list, log, or panel must be able to state its paging / limit / bounded semantics; performance reviews use the fixed user performanceadmin, the work root .wunderperf, and a 5s command timeout. Changelog and lessons-learned docs/功能迭代.md: each round's changes go into a designated category block. The types are: added / changed / fixed / performance / docs / refactor / security / engineering / testing / removed / deprecated. docs/经验教训.md: for recurring problems, you must write an entry after fixing one, so the same mistake isn't repeated. Project SOP docs/SOP.md: a 6-step flow (worktree → quality-gate → peer review → merge-gate → PR → merge and cleanup); Biome pnpm check, pnpm lint; files warn at 200 lines and hard-cap at 350. Reading paths New users: user manual → Quick Start → Pupa intro; when something goes wrong, first-run troubleshooting. Developers getting started: technical manual 01–03 → 02 repository structure and modules → 03 runtime and execution path; then design docs 01–02 to fill in the "why." Adding an interface: technical manual 07 → API reference → design doc 07. Performance issues: performance standards → performance scoring → performance baselines; for specific paging constants, see technical manual 03–04. Operations and acceptance: technical manual 10 → docs/SOP.md; docs/功能迭代.md for historical decisions; docs/经验教训.md to avoid repeating pitfalls. text: First-Run Troubleshooting The failure modes and verification points for the first launch or deployment of each form: Pupa startup, Hull deployment, Beehive access, Helm execution. # First-Run Troubleshooting Sections are organized by form. Each section's verification points are a health checklist for that form; the failure table gives what to check first and where to go next. Pupa (desktop) Verification points After wunder-frontend-slint starts you land in the workbench, with no local listening port at all /.wunder/workspace and /config/desktop.settings.json have been created Settings → Model: "Test connection" returns success The first message shows tool batches and a final reply Failure symptoms and where to check | Symptom | Check first | Docs | | --- | --- | --- | | The startup screen never finishes | Permissions on /.wunder; work-tree scan duration (up to 4096 items) | Pupa intro | | The window appears but the workspace is empty | Whether the working-directory area shows "offline" | Pupa interface | | Model request 401/403 | Settings → Model → API key and endpoint URL; rerun "Test connection" | Configuration reference | | Sending a message during a run is rejected as "user busy" | The session queue is on by default; turning it off breaks the queue bar | Quick Start | | Expecting TTS playback but hearing nothing | Pupa TTS is not implemented — only the model can be configured; use the Beehive for TTS | Pupa interface | | Can't find a "device interlink" settings category | The category isn't wired to the interface; the available surfaces are only the sidebar's cloud workspaces plus the remote command approval dialog | Surfaces overview | | State is a mess | Settings → General → one-click workspace state reset (keeps skills, knowledge bases, long-term memory, configuration, and workspace files) | Pupa intro | Hull (server) Verification points docker compose ps shows everything running: wunder-server, wunder-nginx, postgres, sandbox, onlyoffice, drawio, extra-mcp all present Health check: GET http:// :18000/wunder/i18n returns 200 Bridge: opening http:// :18000/ in a browser shows the "4 groups / 19 items" top-level navigation Beehive: opening http:// :18001/ in a browser reaches the login page Failure symptoms and where to check | Symptom | Check first | Docs | | --- | --- | --- | | Port 18000 unreachable | WUNDERHOST / WUNDERPORT overrides; the server section of config/wunder.yaml | Hull deployment | | The Bridge loads but 18001 (Beehive) is blank | Whether the Beehive frontend was built (frontend/dist); whether the web-service container is up; docker compose logs wunder-nginx | Hull deployment | | Opening 18000 shows the Beehive's look | The two concepts got mixed up — the Hull only mounts the Bridge static pages; the Beehive's frontend/dist is delivered by a standalone web-service container on 18001, not hosted by the Hull | Surfaces overview | | Loading the example config at startup silently fails and falls back to defaults | Known issue; point explicitly at config/wunder.yaml, or use WUNDERCONFIGPATH | Configuration reference | | Client WebSocket keeps hitting slowclient | Slow-client backpressure (queue watermark 2); first check whether long messages are involved | Troubleshooting | | PostgreSQL connection failure | WUNDERPOSTGRESDSN / WUNDERPOSTGRESPOOLSIZE; whether the postgres service is healthy | Hull deployment | | Want to switch back to SQLite | WUNDERSTORAGEBACKEND=sqlite + WUNDERSQLITEDBPATH=/path/to/wunder.db | Configuration reference | | Started in sandbox mode and it listens on 9001 | Normal: sandbox mode takes a different path | Hull deployment | Beehive (web) Verification points The browser opens http:// :18001/ (the web-service container) After a successful login it navigates to /app/chat automatically The composer's "used/capacity" indicator updates normally "Work process" entries in the timeline can be expanded Failure symptoms and where to check | Symptom | Check first | Docs | | --- | --- | --- | | Stuck in a /login loop after opening | Login tokens are opaque random strings, not JWTs; replaying one triggers whole-family revocation | Authentication and security | | Long threads open slowly, rendering stutters | The high-volume thread rendering optimization plan has not landed yet; the performance bottleneck remains | Beehive interface | | WebSocket drops and doesn't recover | After a disconnect, replay endpoints can backfill; the Beehive reuses a single /chat/ws channel | Beehive interface | | Attachment upload fails | Temporary attachment limit 200 MB, persistent attachments 10 MB | Beehive interface | Helm (cli) Verification points In an interactive terminal, wunder-cli opens the ratatui TUI session Non-TTY (pipe / CI) degrades automatically to a one-shot run and exits cleanly wunder-cli doctor reports green Every line of wunder-cli exec --json "..." is valid JSON Failure symptoms and where to check | Symptom | Check first | Docs | | --- | --- | --- | | The interactive session doesn't start; it exits as a one-shot run instead | Whether stdin/stdout/stderr are all TTYs | Helm usage | | Permission error on /.wunder | Override with WUNDERHOME; the data directory defaults to /.wunder | Helm usage | | Can't find a /cron command | The Helm explicitly turns scheduled tasks off; there is no channel / knowledge / memory / persona management interface either | Helm usage | | JSONL events missing fields | Event names are thread / turn / item.; parse against that contract | Helm usage | | Want to run a single tool in a script | Use wunder-cli tool ... directly; it doesn't go through the agent loop | Helm usage | | A second message during a run is rejected as "user busy" | Expected: the Helm sets config.agentqueue.enabled = false (crates/wunder-cli/runtime.rs) — messages don't queue, they hit the session lock; the engine and the Pupa backend continue to be developed. Lists, logs, and panels all have paging, filtering, or bounded limits. If a page renders a large amount of content at once and stutters, that is a known engineering gap — report it. title: Troubleshooting
summary: Three health checks, checks listed by symptom, and what to include when reporting an issue.
headings: Service Starts but Features Are Unavailable
Real-time Status Not Updating, No Intermediate Steps Visible
Tools Don't Appear or Can't Be Called
Attachment Uploaded but Can't Be Sent
New Thread Button Is Grayed Out
Help Manual Blank or Won't Open
Capturing a Performance Report for Chat Stutter
text: Troubleshooting Three health checks, checks listed by symptom, and what to include when reporting an issue. Find the cause by symptom, then read the logs. Health check 1. Make sure the service is running and the page opens. 2. Make sure you can sign in and your account and password are correct. 3. Make sure the model is configured correctly and the API key works. Symptoms and Checks Login Fails or Access Denied Whether your username and password are correct Whether you used the wrong entry point for the Bridge and the Beehive Whether your account is disabled Configuration Changes Not Taking Effect Whether you edited the right configuration file Whether the change needs a service restart Whether the running instance actually loaded the changed configuration Service Starts but Features Are Unavailable Whether the database is connected properly Whether the external tool services (MCP, A2A) are online Whether the sandbox service is reachable Real-time Status Not Updating, No Intermediate Steps Visible Whether your network connection is stable Whether WebSocket is being blocked by a firewall or proxy Whether it recovers after refreshing the page Tools Don't Appear or Can't Be Called Whether the tool is enabled Whether the MCP / A2A service is running Whether the current agent has that tool mounted Whether it is waiting for approval and you missed the prompt Attachment Uploaded but Can't Be Sent Whether the file type is supported (images, audio, video, common documents) Whether the file is still being processed (the send button stays disabled until processing finishes) Whether the workspace has write permission Password Recovery On the login page, click "Reset Password". Required: Username Email New password No old password is required, and you don't need to sign in first. Password Change Won't Save Whether you entered your current password (changing a password while signed in always verifies the old one) Whether the new password and the confirmation match Whether the new password is the same as the current one New Thread Button Is Grayed Out The button is briefly disabled while a thread is being created or switched. Threads running in the background can still start or switch, and an existing unused empty thread is reused first. Session State Completely Messed Up Use "System Settings → Reset Working State": Stop running sessions and tasks Rebuild clean threads It does not delete skills, knowledge bases, or other long-term assets. Microphone or Screenshot Button Unavailable Whether you are in an environment that supports these features Whether the browser has been granted microphone/screen permission Whether the desktop bridge is working properly Help Manual Blank or Won't Open Whether the docs site has been built Whether the reverse proxy is configured correctly for the /docs/ path Capturing a Performance Report for Chat Stutter Open "More → Settings → Performance Capture": 1. Click "Start", then return to chat and reproduce the stutter while replying, scrolling, or switching pages. 2. Go back to settings and click "Download JSON"; the browser downloads the report directly, ready to attach to your issue report. 3. Click "Stop" to end capture. You can still download afterward; starting again creates a new report. No console or reload is needed to start. If you reload the page yourself, this tab keeps capturing and retains the statistics from before the reload, for up to 30 minutes. Browser metrics that aren't supported are marked unavailable. The report includes frame gaps, main-thread long tasks, slower input events, chat rendering and loading timings, periodically sampled DOM/memory peaks, and the browser and app versions. It excludes message bodies, call arguments, accounts, session identifiers, and file paths. Downloading doesn't end capture and doesn't upload any file. When you submit, add what you did and when the stutter happened. Total model reply time and Worker wait time are not the same as main-thread stutter, and the report lists them separately. Still Unresolved When a symptom isn't covered here, continue with the Configuration Reference. Issue Report Contents Include these when reporting an issue: Runtime form: desktop / server / cli Steps that reproduce the problem Key error messages Whether it involves subagents, MCP, A2A, etc. Health check Symptoms and Checks Login Fails or Access Denied Configuration Changes Not Taking Effect Service Starts but Features Are Unavailable Real-time Status Not Updating, No Intermediate Steps Visible Tools Don't Appear or Can't Be Called Attachment Uploaded but Can't Be Sent Password Recovery Password Change Won't Save New Thread Button Is Grayed Out Session State Completely Messed Up Microphone or Screenshot Button Unavailable Help Manual Blank or Won't Open Capturing a Performance Report for Chat Stutter Still Unresolved Issue Report Contents

title: FAQ
summary: Common conclusions on registration, usage, requirement scope, memory loading, the thread button, subagents, passwords, and tool visibility.
headings: When the New Thread Button Is Disabled
Difference Between webfetch and the Browser Tool
Where to Look When Something Goes Wrong
text: FAQ Common conclusions on registration, usage, requirement scope, memory loading, the thread button, subagents, passwords, and tool visibility. ## Registration and Sign-in No registration is required. You can start a conversation under any name, and the system creates the matching identity automatically. Cost and Usage The token count is not the cost. It only reflects the context length of the current conversation; the actual cost depends on your model provider's billing rules. Scope of Requirement Settings Requirements set at the start of a conversation are remembered and locked in. Later messages follow them, so you don't need to repeat them. When Memory Loads Long-term memory loads once, at the start of a conversation. It is not re-read on every turn. When the New Thread Button Is Disabled The button is briefly disabled while a thread is being created or switched. Threads already running in the background do not block a new thread, and an existing unused empty thread is reused first. Subagents A subagent is a temporary work unit the agent creates during a task, used to split off work that can proceed in parallel and get it done; once the result is returned to the main thread, the subagent is reclaimed. It is not a separate agent — on the user side there is always exactly one agent instance. Pupa and Hull Dependency Deploying the Hull is not required. The Pupa can run locally on its own; deploy the Hull when you need multi-person collaboration and unified management. Changing Your Username and Password Change them under "My Profile → Edit". Changing your password requires entering your current password. Password Recovery On the login page, click "Reset Password". You need your username, email, and a new password — no old password required. Cleanup of Uploaded Files Files in the temporary directory may be cleaned up. Keep important files in the workspace's persistent directory. Tool Visibility Possible causes: the tool is not enabled, the MCP/A2A service is not running, or the current agent does not have that tool mounted. Difference Between webfetch and the Browser Tool webfetch: grabs the main text content of a webpage The browser tool: operates a webpage like a real person (clicking, scrolling, filling forms) Where to Look When Something Goes Wrong Symptom-level troubleshooting lives in Troubleshooting. title: Glossary
summary: Form and layer names in wunder, plus definitions for threads, turns, workspaces, and other core terms.
text: Glossary Form and layer names in wunder, plus definitions for threads, turns, workspaces, and other core terms. ## Product and Form Names | Name | Short id | Meaning | |------|------|------| | wunder | wunder | The product itself, the umbrella term for the agent orchestration platform: hand a goal to the agent, and it breaks the task down, calls tools, and delivers results. | | Core | core | The foundation: configuration, authentication, storage, and execution policy. | | Engine | runtime | The execution layer: task orchestration, thread runtime, tools, channels, and gateway. The Pupa and the Helm depend on the Engine directly, not on the Hull. | | Hull | server | The user and agent management platform: the server form, aimed at teams and organizations, handling multi-user access, permissions, and channel access, and providing the Beehive. | | Bridge | bridge | The governance frontend: the system administrator's management interface for system configuration and for user and channel governance. | | Bridge node | bridge node | A channel bridging node: it carries channel account access and message routing and is managed uniformly by the backend, with no standalone frontend page today. Keep it distinct from the governance frontend "Bridge". | | Beehive | web | The cloud AI workbench: the web form, provided with the Hull and opened by users in a browser. | | Pupa | desktop | The local AI workbench: the desktop form, the default entry point for individual users, running locally with direct access to local files. Formerly Honeycomb. | | Helm | cli | The manual local entry point: the command-line form, aimed at hands-on operation, developers, and automation scripts. | Hull, Bridge, Beehive, Pupa, and Helm name concrete forms of wunder; Core and Engine name the underlying layers. Keep the two groups separate. The first mention in the body pairs a form's display name with its short id — for example Hull (server), Pupa (desktop), Helm (cli). User Your identity marker. It can be a registered account or a temporary virtual name; the system recognizes both. Agent The AI role that executes tasks. An agent has its own model, tools, and prompt configuration. Every user has exactly one agent instance, generated from a 1:1 binding to an admin-side preset; there is no user-side entry point to create, delete, switch, or reorder agents, and only the fields a preset marks as customizable can be changed. Preset Agent An agent template maintained by the admin. There can be several presets, but each user binds exactly one of them, which generates that user's single agent instance. Applying a preset updates its system-managed configuration only for bound users and preserves user-created MCP, skills, and knowledge-base selection states. Thread One continuous conversation. One agent can have several threads, and each thread maintains its own context independently. Subagent A temporary work unit the main agent creates during a task and reclaims once the task is done. It is not a separate agent, and not a second agent the user owns. Workspace Your persistent file space. Every user has exactly one workspace, which tools use as their root: in the Pupa (desktop) it is a persistent directory on your own machine, with direct read and write access to local files; in a Hull (server) deployment it is the single per-user directory under the server data root, reached through the Beehive. A workspace cannot be added, deleted, or replaced. Working Directory The workspace entry point in the UI: below the workspace in the left column of the web app, holding a file tree, a toolbar (upload / new / refresh / multi-select), a usage bar, and a preview overlay. It is not an operating-system file browser. User Turn Every message a user sends is one user turn. Model Turn Every action the model takes (thinking, calling a tool, replying) is one model turn. One user turn may contain several model turns. Skill A capability package for the model. It usually contains documentation, scripts, and resource files that let an agent handle specific types of tasks. MCP Model Context Protocol. A standard interface that lets wunder connect to external tool services. A2A An interoperability protocol between agents. It lets agents from different systems discover and collaborate with each other. Channel An external messaging path, such as Feishu, WeCom, QQ, or XMPP. Through channels, an agent can send and receive external messages. Token The basic unit by which a model processes text. The token count reflects the current conversation's context length and does not equal the actual cost. Context Compression When a conversation gets too long, the system automatically compresses the history so the model can keep working without losing key information. Long-term Memory Knowledge an agent remembers across conversations. You can add it manually, or let the system distill it automatically. Product and Form Names User Agent Preset Agent Thread Subagent Workspace Working Directory User Turn Model Turn Skill MCP A2A Channel Token Context Compression Long-term Memory

title: Tools Overview
summary: Canonical names and English aliases of the built-in tools, the doc pages for each of the eight categories, situations mapped to tools, and the shared result shell plus the exceptions that skip it.
text: Tools Overview Canonical names and English aliases of the built-in tools, the doc pages for each of the eight categories, situations mapped to tools, and the shared result shell plus the exceptions that skip it. Canonical tool names the model sees are mostly Chinese, each paired with an English alias, normalized by resolvetoolname (crates/wunder-runtime/src/services/tools/catalog.rs). MCP tools (server@tool), skill names, knowledge-base names, and user tool aliases are registered dynamically from configuration and are not in the table below. The tool matrix | 工具（规范名） | 英文别名 | 简介 | 分类 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 计划面板 | updateplan | 向前端推送结构化的任务计划面板 | 收尾与前端协同 | | 问询面板 | questionpanel | 弹出结构化选项，向用户提问并等待选择 | 收尾与前端协同 | | 会话让出 | sessionsyield | 主动让出当前回合控制权，稍后再被唤起 | 收尾与前端协同 | | 列出文件 | listfiles | 列出目录内容 | 工作区与代码 | | glob | — | 按通配模式查找文件路径 | 工作区与代码 | | 搜索内容 | searchcontent | 在文件中按正则搜索匹配内容 | 工作区与代码 | | 读取文件 | readfile | 读取文件内容，支持分段读取 | 工作区与代码 | | 写入文件 | writefile | 写入或整体覆盖文件 | 工作区与代码 | | 文本编辑 | edit / editfile | 精确替换 / 补丁 / 子命令三形态（applypatch 已并入） | 工作区与代码 | | 执行命令 | executecommand | 执行 Shell / 系统命令 | 工作区与代码 | | 命令会话 | commandsession | 管理后台长驻命令会话，支持前后台切换 | 工作区与代码 | | 技能调用 | skillcall | 读取技能正文并执行技能脚本 | 工作区与代码 | | 网页抓取 | webfetch | 抓取并解析网页正文（需启用配置） | Web | | 浏览器 | browser | 聚合展示名；底层为 17 个 browser 原生工具（点击、输入、等待、截图等） | Web | | 读图工具 | readimage | 读取图片内容供模型理解（需 vision 能力） | 多模态 | | 图像生成 | generateimage | 按提示词生成图片 | 多模态 | | 视频生成 | generatevideo | 按提示词生成视频 | 多模态 | | 语音生成 | generatespeech | 文本转语音 | 多模态 | | 声转文 | transcribespeech | 语音转文字 | 多模态 | | 桌面控制 | desktopcontrol | 操作本机桌面并观察（鼠标、键盘、窗口） | 桌面 | | 子智能体控制 | subagentcontrol | 在任务中临时派生子智能体，结果回传后回收 | 线程与子智能体 | | 会话线程控制 | threadcontrol | 管理任务线程 / 分支线程（桌面端不开放） | 线程与子智能体 | | 自我状态 | selfstatus | 查询智能体自身的运行状态 | 系统与记忆 | | 记忆管理 | memorymanager | 读写长期记忆 | 系统与记忆 | | 定时任务 | scheduletask | 创建与管理定时 / 周期任务 | 系统与记忆 | | getgoal / creategoal / updategoal | — | 目标态三件套，由运行时按会话自动注入，不对桌面端开放选择 | 目标态 | 网页搜索 and ptc are retained in code but currently temporarily delisted — invisible to the model and to the user (see defaulttoolprofile.rs); they are not removed. Removed entirely: channel tools, user-world tools, a2a tools, finalresponse, a2ui, LSP query tools. Situations and tools | Situation | Use | | --- | --- | | You have a URL and want that page's body | Web Fetch | | You only have keywords and need a public web source | Web search is currently delisted; once you have a URL, use Web Fetch | | You need to click, type, or wait for dynamic rendering | Browser | | Looking at local code | List directories or search with Workspace Files first, then read the ranges you need | | A small, precise, context-matched code edit | the patch form of 文本编辑 | | One exact text replacement | 文本编辑 in Workspace Files | | Complex replacement logic | run a script with Execute Command | | Rewriting or creating a whole file | writefile in Workspace Files | | Compiling, testing, or running a script | Execute Command | | Spinning up a temporary child run in the current session | Subagent Control | | Managing the task thread or branch threads | Thread Control | Categories and docs | Category | Pages | | --- | --- | | Turn finishing and frontend coordination | Plan Panel / Question Panel / Sessions Yield: Plan Panel / Question Panel / Sessions Yield | | Workspace and code | List files / glob / search content / read file / write file / text edit: Workspace Files; execute command / command session: Execute Command; skill call: Skill Call | | Web | Web fetch: Web Fetch; browser: Browser Tools | | Multimodal | Read image: Read Image; generate image / generate video / generate speech / transcribe speech: canonical names 图像生成 / 视频生成 / 语音生成 / 声转文, aliases generateimage / generatevideo / generatespeech / transcribespeech; no dedicated page in this section | | Desktop | Desktop control: Desktop Control | | Threads and subagents | Subagent control: Subagent Control; thread control: Thread Control | | System and memory | Self status: Self Status; memory manager: Memory Manager; schedule task: Schedule Task | | Goal state | getgoal / creategoal / updategoal are injected by the runtime per session, and not offered for selection on the desktop endpoint | Result shell Most built-in tools return the same shell on success: whether it succeeded, the action name, a state, a one-line summary, and a data area that carries the business result. Read the business result from the data area first. Some tools add one more line telling you what to do next. Common states include: completed, dry run only, accepted, running, yielded, awaiting input, partially complete, timed out, and no change. A timeout does not always mean a permanent failure. Failures use the same shell: an error line, a readable reason and fix hint, and data that helps with diagnosis. Exceptions that skip the shared shell: Final Response (removed): only a termination signal, returning a single answer to the user. Schedule Task: returns a compact scheduling result. Browser tool group: results use a content-block structure (see Browser). Web Search (delisted): used to search the public web by keyword, with results in the data area's results field; to read a page now, use Web Fetch directly. Web Fetch: returns the fetched result object directly on success. Text Edit (formerly applypatch): success uses the shared shell; in its patch form, failures carry stricter error semantics than ordinary file tools. title: Plan Panel / Question Panel / Sessions Yield
summary: Aliases of the three interaction-control tools, their argument limits and normalized spellings, the replacement and turn-ending semantics that apply at call time, and their item caps.
text: Plan Panel / Question Panel / Sessions Yield Aliases of the three interaction-control tools, their argument limits and normalized spellings, the replacement and turn-ending semantics that apply at call time, and their item caps. The three tools belong to the same interaction-control family. None of them produces a business side effect; they only change what the frontend shows or how the current turn ends. | Canonical name | Aliases | | --- | --- | | 计划面板 | updateplan | | 问询面板 | questionpanel, askpanel | | 会话让出 | sessionsyield, yield | The standalone "sleep and wait" tool has also been deleted, and waiting semantics are now carried by 会话让出. Plan Panel Use it to build and maintain an execution checklist when a task takes several steps and the user wants to follow progress. Work that finishes in one go does not need a plan. A plan is a set of steps, 1 to 12 items, each a step plus a status; items with an empty step are dropped. Statuses are pending / inprogress / completed, and variants such as in-progress, done, and complete are normalized. You can attach one line describing the change to the plan. The call replaces the whole plan rather than patching it. Only one step may be in progress at a time; if a second one appears, it is downgraded to pending. An empty plan, or one whose steps are all dropped, reports an error. The result does not echo the plan content back; the plan reaches the user through a frontend event. Question Panel Use it when several reasonable routes exist and the user has to decide before work continues. Opening the panel hands the current turn to the user, so do not keep assuming an answer within the same turn. It can ask 1 to 4 questions, each with 1 to 4 options; an option can be a label plus description plus a recommended flag, or just a string. Each question can be set to multiple choice, single choice by default. The old flat single-question form (question, options, and a multiple-choice flag at the top level) is still accepted. An option whose label contains "recommended", or that carries the recommended flag, is recognized as the recommended choice. More than 4 questions keeps only the first 4; a question with no options is dropped entirely; if everything is dropped, it reports an error. The panel is sent in a "stay open" form, and the turn ends there: the closing text tells the user to answer in the panel, and the stop reason is recorded as the question panel: opening the panel ends the turn and waits for the user's next message. Sessions Yield Use it when the turn has nothing left to do but you want to state explicitly that you are yielding and waiting for an external event, rather than hard-coding a closing line. It is not a substitute for a final reply, nor a timer. Waking on schedule is handled by Schedule Task. You can give one line of yield note to tell the user the current state; leaving it empty uses the default waiting text. The result state is "yielded", the turn's answer is set to that note, and the stop reason is recorded as a yield. In desktop mode (Pupa) 会话让出 is listed as a hidden tool and is not exposed to the agent. Errors All three use the shared failure shell. The most common failures are argument validation: an empty plan in the Plan Panel, no usable options in the Question Panel, and parse errors from a malformed argument structure. Boundaries Panels neither authenticate nor approve: they only handle presentation and turn control, and have nothing to do with the approval tier for writing files or running commands. The results of the plan and the question are deliberately thin, to save context; do not stuff detailed content into the note for the model to read back. When the frontend stream drops, panel events may not render, but the turn-ending semantics still take effect: after a question or a yield, do not expect the same turn to continue. Limits: at most 12 plan items, at most 4 questions, and at most 4 options per question; anything beyond is rejected or trimmed. Plan Panel Question Panel Sessions Yield Errors Boundaries

title: Workspace Files
summary: Parameters, matching rules, and failure diagnosis for the five operations: list a directory, search content, read a range, exact replacement, and whole-file write.
