Command sessions adapt to old terminals: command sessions are carried over winpty, and output is decoded as GBK. Startup checks: a recovery scan and self-check run at startup. Both chains work offline, the interface needs no GPU, and command sessions adapt to legacy terminals — Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04 (x64 / arm64) can run the Pupa and the Helm directly. Limits Build scripts still carry dead Tauri links, pointing at directories that no longer exist. That is an engineering gap, not a capability. win7 interlink nodes do not declare tool.exec, so the capability surface on legacy devices is narrower. Compatibility Supported systems Runtime constraints Limits

title: Context Compression
summary: The four graded compression levels triggered when the context window is exceeded, what compression protects and leaves alone, compression records, and the local-reduction path that comes first.
text: Context Compression The four graded compression levels triggered when the context window is exceeded, what compression protects and leaves alone, compression records, and the local-reduction path that comes first. How much history a single conversation can carry is set by the model's context window. As a conversation grows, the total of history plus tool results can exceed the ceiling, and compression trims the history without interrupting the conversation so it keeps running. Compression is not deletion. Deletion cuts content outright, regardless of importance; compression reorganizes content, keeping the key facts and trimming the redundant parts. Triggers These situations tend to trigger compression: a very long conversation (dozens of rounds or more), a tool returning a large amount of content (reading a large file, many search results), and complex multi-step tasks. To trigger it less often, open a new thread once a topic is done rather than keeping an old thread alive, keep prompts concise, and avoid pasting large repeated blocks; the /compact command triggers compression deliberately. Levels Compression escalates from gentle to aggressive only when necessary: | Level | Strategy | Degree of loss | | --- | --- | --- | | Level 1 | Remove intermediate tool results | Very low; tool results can be fetched again | | Level 2 | Summarize historical messages | Medium; keeps semantics, loses detail | | Level 3 | Remove earlier conversation rounds | Higher; keeps only the most recent content | | Level 4 | Keep only the core setup and the current request | Very high; emergency degradation | What is protected Without compression, a long conversation ends in one of three ways: an outright error, a brute-force truncation, or manual control of conversation length. Compression is a system capability, so conversation length needs no manual management. Compression protects three things first: the continuity of the conversation, so it is not interrupted for being too long; the facts genuinely needed, favoring information useful to the current task; and traceability, so every compression leaves a record of what it compressed and what it kept for administrators to inspect. There are two bottom lines. First, compression can only trim and reorganize existing content; it never invents. Second, a thread's core setup (the system prompt) is frozen at creation, and compression acts only on the conversation history and tool results, so an agent never "forgets who it is" because of compression. Compression records Every compression leaves a record that includes the strategy used, the context size before and after, and a rough assessment of the information lost. Administrators use it to judge whether compression has affected task quality. Local reduction When automatic compression triggers, the system first sees whether earlier file reads, searches, and listing results can be shortened. The last 5 groups of tool results, error information, media, and results that still need pagination are protected. A shortened old result still carries its location, a head/tail preview, and an explicit omission notice, so the agent can read it again when needed. If the local reduction has already freed enough space, no extra model call is made to produce a summary; if not, the summary flow runs. Manual compression and overflow recovery go straight to summarization. A summary outputs at most 2048 tokens by default, and if the model itself is configured with a smaller output limit, the smaller one wins. Administrators can see the estimated savings of the local reduction in the progress records. The estimate is for diagnosis only; actual token consumption follows the model provider's report. Limits After compression, the system favors what the current task needs. Only in extreme cases (a very long conversation stacked with a large amount of tool output) might the agent recall early details less precisely, and then a new conversation thread is the fix. Triggers Levels What is protected Compression records Local reduction Limits

title: Subagents
summary: The 11 actions of Subagent Control, the `user_round` + `model_round` parent–child round references, and the removal of swarm orchestration from the engine and protocol layer.
text: Subagents The 11 actions of Subagent Control, the userround + modelround parent–child round references, and the removal of swarm orchestration from the engine and protocol layer. # Subagents The parent thread hands one subtask to an independent executor, which runs it and passes the result back to the parent thread. Control actions 子智能体控制 (Subagent Control) provides 11 actions: | Action | Action | Action | | --- | --- | --- | | spawn | batchspawn | wait | | interrupt | close | resume | | report | send | status | | list | history | | Parent–child round references are encoded as userround + modelround, and an executor's rounds hang under that pair of parent round references. The sub-session's user message is hidden, and it wakes with auto-wake. Limits The only collaborative form is the subagent. Swarm orchestration (swarm tools, hives, orchestration mode, team runs, swarm packs) has been removed from the engine and the protocol layer; it is not waiting to be implemented, nor hidden behind a switch. Swarm leftovers remain in TUI prompts, front-end i18n labels, and compatibility shims, and empty directories await cleanup. Those leftovers do not mean the capability exists. Subagents Control actions Limits

title: Scheduled Tasks
summary: The semantics and bounds of the at, every, and cron schedule kinds, the two delivery targets, lease, backoff, and auto-disable parameters, and support by form.
headings: Entry points and support by form
text: Scheduled Tasks The semantics and bounds of the at, every, and cron schedule kinds, the two delivery targets, lease, backoff, and auto-disable parameters, and support by form. The task definition is persisted in storage, and a background loop claims work by due time, independent of which session you happen to be viewing. Every run is recorded (/wunder/cron/runs): whether it ran, whether it succeeded, and when it will run next; failures come with backoff and auto-disable; and a process restart does not lose the task definitions. This differs from waiting inside a session: yielding in a session only affects the current thread, whereas a scheduled task creates a new run in the future. Scheduled tasks diagram: scheduling rules enter the scheduler, then dispatch to background execution and execution records Schedule kinds The kind field is one of at, every, or cron. | Kind | Semantics | Input | Bounds | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | at | One-off point in time | An RFC3339 timestamp | At most 365 days ahead; auto-disabled once it runs (disabled with a reason if it fails) | | every | Fixed interval | everyms (optional start time) | 1,000 ms ≤ interval ≤ 86,400,000 ms (24 hours) | | cron | Recurring expression | A 5–7 field expression plus an optional timezone | Fields accept only digits and / - , ?; the timezone is parsed as a named timezone, defaulting to the local timezone | Natural language also works in tools and quick input, and the system converts it into the kinds above: every 5 minutes becomes a fixed interval, and daily at 9am and weekdays at 6pm become the corresponding cron expressions; when it cannot parse the input, it suggests the formats that are accepted. Content limits: a task name is at most 128 characters, and a trigger message at most 16,384 characters. Result delivery sessiontarget has two values. | Value | Behavior | | --- | --- | | main (default) | The result is delivered to the bound current session, continuing the same conversation | | isolated | Each run creates a separate thread session and keeps a link back to the parent session | Choose isolated for recurring tasks that need a trail and should not disturb the main conversation; choose main when you want the result appended directly to the existing context. Execution guarantees In multi-instance deployments a lease prevents duplicate execution: when a task is claimed, the runner's identity, a run token, and a lease expiry are written, and the lease is renewed with a heartbeat while the run lasts; if the process crashes, the lease expires and another instance can claim the task. Each record also carries a deduplication key and a consecutive-failure count, and writes down why it was disabled. Default scheduling parameters: | Parameter | Default | | --- | --- | | Max concurrent runs | 1 | | Poll interval | 1000 ms | | Max idle sleep | 5000 ms | | Lease lifetime / heartbeat | 300 seconds / 60 seconds | | Consecutive-failure auto-disable threshold | 5 | After a failure, backoff steps up with the consecutive-failure count: 30 seconds → 60 seconds → 5 minutes → 15 minutes → 1 hour, then stays at the last step. Once the failure limit is reached, the task is auto-disabled with a written reason; re-enabling it resets the failure count. Master switch With the master switch off (cron.enabled=false), four kinds of write operation are rejected: add, update, enable, and run, each with a clear message. Status, list, a single detail, run records, delete, and disable all remain available, so existing tasks can still be reviewed and cleaned up. Entry points and support by form | Surface | Status | | --- | --- | | API | /wunder/cron/, 11 endpoints in all (status / list / runs / add / update / remove / enable / disable / get / run / action), on the user side, isolated by user ownership | | Tool | The built-in scheduled-tasks tool (canonical name 定时任务, alias scheduletask), sharing the same handler as the API, so the model can create tasks on its own | | Beehive | A scheduled-tasks category page under settings | | Pupa | A scheduled-tasks page plus a native entry point, calling the same handler in-process | | Helm | No scheduled tasks: the local engine explicitly disables the scheduler at startup, and there is no related slash command | | Bridge | No user-level task management page; it exists only as a template configuration under preset agents | When you need something to run on a schedule, configure it on the Beehive, the Pupa, or the Hull side. Schedule kinds Result delivery Execution guarantees Master switch Entry points and support by form

title: Channels
summary: The support level of Feishu, QQ, WeChat, XMPP, and generic webhooks; the binding score that routes a message to its agent and workspace; inbound, outbound, and rate-limit parameters.
text: Channels The support level of Feishu, QQ, WeChat, XMPP, and generic webhooks; the binding score that routes a message to its agent and workspace; inbound, outbound, and rate-limit parameters. ## Scope of responsibility All execution happens in the engine. A channel does just two things: parse an external message into a unified inbound shape, and deliver the unified outbound shape back into an external protocol. Protocol adaptation stops at the entry; a channel does not copy business logic, does not keep its own storage, and does not change thread semantics. The same task thread can take a message from Beehive, continue it from Feishu, and finish it from Pupa; a channel never creates a second execution path. A form (Pupa / Beehive / Helm / Hull) is the shape of running and access; a channel (Feishu / QQ / WeChat …) is an off-site platform. The two are not one layer. The statement that many entries share one engine holds; what tends to be written wrong is the support level. Support level Feishu (feishu): a persistent connection plus a webhook, fully implemented, with a dedicated webhook entry point. QQ Bot (qqbot): a persistent connection plus a webhook, fully implemented, with a dedicated webhook entry point. WeChat (weixin): runs on a persistent connection (iLink long polling), fully implemented, and the largest in scale. XMPP (xmpp): a persistent connection plus a webhook. It is disabled by default and is only a placeholder then, returning a "not enabled" notice for all send and receive; it becomes a real implementation only once explicitly turned on. WeCom (wechat): webhook only, partially implemented (send, receive, and signature verification), with no persistent connection. WeChat Official Account (wechatmp): webhook only, partially implemented, with no persistent connection. WhatsApp Cloud (whatsappcloud): webhook only, partially implemented, with no persistent connection. Only four channels use a persistent connection: Feishu, QQ Bot, XMPP, and WeChat (weixin). WeCom, the Official Account, and WhatsApp Cloud are pure webhook callbacks. The following platforms have no adapter at all: telegram, discord, slack, LINE, DingTalk. They exist only as generic-webhook directory entries, handled through the generic entry point and generic parsing — with no platform-specific signature verification, rich-text mapping, attachment download, or proactive push. The accurate statement is that they are visible in the directory and can send and receive text over a generic webhook, but they have no platform-specific adapter. Writing them up as "supported channels" is wrong. Binding resolution An inbound message is first resolved by binding: candidates are scored by specificity, the single best one is taken, and priority breaks a tie. | Dimension | Score | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Exact peerid match | 8 | Supports the wildcard, and a wildcard scores nothing | | peerkind match | 4 | dm/direct/single/user are treated as the same kind | | accountid match | 2 | Empty means wildcard | | channel match | 1 | Empty means wildcard | A hit yields the target agent and any tool overrides, after which the workspace is decided: empty, as well as the default and default aliases, all point to that user's default agent workspace. In the Hull form, workspaces are flattened per user into a single cloud directory, so files arriving from different channels for the same user land in the same place. Inbound, outbound, and rate limiting Inbound uses a bounded queue: capacity 512, concurrency 8, enqueue timeout 80 ms. A full queue or an enqueue timeout counts as backpressure and reports "queue busy" rather than piling up without limit. The visible effect is that the platform redelivers or briefly delays; messages are not silently dropped. Outbound runs on a persistent queue with exponential backoff, defaulting to a 500 ms polling interval, batches of 50, and at most 5 retries, with a backoff base of 2 s and a ceiling of 60 s. Outbound delivery has a switch. When it is off, delivery is instead attempted once synchronously at enqueue time and is no longer redelivered by the polling loop. When troubleshooting a "received but no reply" case, check this switch first: once it is off and that one synchronous attempt fails, the message sits in the outbound queue waiting for manual handling. Rate limiting is a token bucket of QPS plus a concurrency cap per channel account; both at 0 means no limiting. A rate-limited request does not consume a concurrency slot and is handed to the outbound queue for backoff redelivery. Attachments and media Inbound media is downloaded, transcoded, and dropped into the workspace for that channel before being handed to the engine; platform-specific files have their own download entry points and likewise write into the workspace; and a further kind of pending file is reserved first and fetched on demand. Outbound attachments are extracted from the body, from Markdown, or from a workspace path and then uploaded. Channel clients usually do not understand internal paths, so attachments go out as an upload link rather than a path string thrown at the user. Webhook entry points and verification The generic entry point is POST /wunder/channel/{provider}/webhook; Feishu and QQ Bot have their own dedicated entry points at POST /wunder/channel/feishu/webhook and POST /wunder/channel/qqbot/webhook. Verification differs by platform: some loop back a verification token from configuration, some use a content signature, and WeCom additionally verifies the signature and decrypts the encrypted message. The generic webhook does no platform-specific verification, so platforms that use the generic entry point need to close this off themselves at a gateway or reverse proxy to guarantee a trustworthy source. Troubleshooting messages 1. Presence: for a persistent-connection channel, check whether its connection process is running; a webhook-only channel has no notion of presence, so check only whether the callback arrives. 2. Whether the callback arrives: check the platform-side push logs and the channel's runtime logs. 3. Whether it was routed: check the binding score and the enabled state; a binding to a different agent looks exactly like no response at all. 4. Arrived but no reply: check for records stuck in the outbound queue, whether the outbound delivery loop is off, and whether rate limiting was hit. 5. XMPP specifics: confirm whether it is enabled — while disabled by default it is only a placeholder, and errors say so directly. Points not to mix up telegram / discord / slack / LINE / DingTalk have no adapter; they are only generic directory entries. WeCom and the Official Account have no persistent connection; only Feishu, QQ Bot, XMPP, and WeChat have one. XMPP is disabled by default, and while disabled it is a placeholder. A channel cannot be configured with business logic; it has only two layers, the target agent and tool overrides, and everything else lives in the engine and on the management side. The core capabilities are the same across channels; the differences are only in protocol expression (rich text, attachments, cards) and whether a persistent connection is supported. The inbound queue does not guarantee no loss by queuing forever; it is bounded at 512 with an 80 ms enqueue timeout, and anything beyond goes to backpressure and platform redelivery. A failed outbound delivery is not dropped outright; it uses a persistent queue with exponential backoff and at most 5 retries. Pupa and Helm do not go through the channel layer: Pupa is a native in-process call, and Helm uses its own access path. Scope of responsibility Support level Binding resolution Inbound, outbound, and rate limiting Attachments and media Webhook entry points and verification Troubleshooting messages Points not to mix up

title: Memory
summary: The two layers in which long-term material is injected once at thread creation and then frozen, how structured fragments are organized, and how memory divides the work with the workspace and the knowledge base.
text: Memory The two layers in which long-term material is injected once at thread creation and then frozen, how structured fragments are organized, and how memory divides the work with the workspace and the knowledge base. An agent needs long-term information — who the user is, what they prefer, what policies an organization has, what background a project has. Such material is injected once when the thread is created and stays frozen afterwards, never rewritten dynamically on every round. Three things follow: cognitive boundaries stay stable while the thread runs, so it does not drift as the conversation goes on; the system prompt stays stable, which helps cache acceleration; and it can clearly answer what background this thread started from. On the user side this shows up as personal preferences taking effect automatically in new conversations and the agent being able to use long-term material in the workspace and knowledge base. On the administrator side it shows up as controllable injection rules, sensitive information not leaking, conversations of the same kind starting from the same background, and a thread's initialization background being traceable. The two layers The first layer is thread-initialization injection. When a thread is created, the system writes the key long-term material into the system prompt, where it becomes the thread's cognitive base. The second layer is runtime supplementary retrieval. If more material is needed during execution, the system retrieves it dynamically through recall rather than rewriting the system prompt. Structure Memory uses structured fragments rather than one long free-text block. Fragments are found by lookup, replaced individually without affecting the rest, marked invalid when outdated, and carry traceable version relationships. Freezing rules Once the system prompt is set it stays frozen, and later conversation never modifies it dynamically, which keeps thread behavior stable. Long-term memory is injected only once at thread creation; even if recall fires during a run, its result is only supplementary reference and never rewrites the system prompt. Division of sources Workspaces, knowledge bases, and memory can all supply material, but their responsibilities differ: | Source | Character | Use | | --- | --- | --- | | Workspace | The scene of the current task | Holds the files being worked on | | Knowledge base | A long-term document source | Retrieves policies, material, and reference documents | | Memory | Structured accumulation | Remembers who the user is, their preferences, and past decisions | When updates take effect When a memory update takes effect depends on the thread: a newly created thread applies the latest memory automatically, while an existing thread is unaffected and keeps the copy from when it was created. After a personal preference is updated, a new conversation is needed for it to take effect. Limits Memory and context compression have different jobs: compression governs near-field information such as conversation history, while memory supplies far-field information such as long-term background. Compression does not touch the memory inside the system prompt. More memory is not better. Injecting too much crowds the conversation's context space, introduces irrelevant information that disturbs judgment, and raises token consumption. The system therefore has selection and limiting mechanisms and does not inject without bound. Points not to mix up Memory does not update automatically every round; it is injected only at initialization and does not change during a run. Recall is a dynamic supplement and does not rewrite the base. Workspace files are not the same as memory either — a workspace is the scene of the current task, while memory is long-term accumulation. The two layers Structure Freezing rules Division of sources When updates take effect Limits Points not to mix up

title: Multi-threading
summary: Scheduling, locks, and realtime state isolated per thread inside one process: the engine-level session queue, a 120-second session lock TTL, tool parallelism ≤ 4, and a round cap of 1000.
text: Multi-threading Scheduling, locks, and realtime state isolated per thread inside one process: the engine-level session queue, a 120-second session lock TTL, tool parallelism ≤ 4, and a round cap of 1000. # Multi-threading A single user can hold several task threads at once, and scheduling, locks, and realtime state are isolated per thread so the threads do not block one another. Concurrency control The engine-level session queue is enabled by default, with 会话让出 as the way to yield. A session lock has a TTL of 120 seconds with heartbeat renewal; when its holder exits abnormally, the TTL releases it. Tool parallelism ≤ 4: tools that run in parallel take a read lock, and tools that run exclusively take a write lock. Round caps, active-session caps, daily quotas, and retry circuit breaking form four hard constraints. Defaults | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Session lock TTL | 120 seconds (with heartbeat) | | Tool parallelism | ≤ 4 | | Round cap | 1000 by default | Limits With agentqueue.enabled turned off, sending another message while a run is in progress is judged "user busy" and no longer enters the queue bar (the Hull warns about this at startup). This is a configuration choice, not a fault. Blocking category quotas and bounded queues are hard caps: when full, the system reports busy and does not wait in a queue. Multi-threading Concurrency control Defaults Limits

title: Multi-user Management
summary: Users, units, and permission boundaries in the Hull form — opaque tokens, presence split by form, the unit tree, levels and credits, worker cards, and data isolation.
text: Multi-user Management Users, units, and permission boundaries in the Hull form — opaque tokens, presence split by form, the unit tree, levels and credits, worker cards, and data isolation. Multi-user governance is a foundational capability of the Hull (server) form; the Pupa (desktop) and the Helm (cli) are local, single-machine forms with no account system. Concrete panel operations are covered in the reference section. Identity checks Management gate: management paths (such as /wunder/admin/) require an API key or a Bearer token on the server side, and the account must be an administrator; a unit head is separately allowed on designated paths. User ownership: a user-facing request is first resolved to a user by Bearer, then its ownership is checked, ensuring it can touch only its own sessions, tools, and tasks. Realtime channels: a WebSocket connection carries a token in its handshake, and each of the six realtime channels authenticates on its own. Tokens | Credential | Shape | Default lifetime | | --- | --- | --- | | Access token | A random string starting with wund, verified by looking it up in the database | 7 days | | Refresh token | A random string starting with wundr | 30 days | | External-login one-time code | Starting with wundc, held in memory | Short-lived | A token is not a self-contained JWT: it carries no claims and cannot be parsed offline. Validation is a database lookup, so revocation takes effect immediately. A few key semantics: Refresh is an OAuth-style family rotation: one refresh issues a new access plus a new refresh, both in the same rotation family; presenting an already-revoked token to refresh again is judged to be a stolen token, and the whole family (including the access token in use) is revoked at once. The session scope decides who can renew: login reads the x-wunder-session-scope header, and only local scopes such as the Pupa and the Helm get a refresh chain that can renew; browser sessions do not take this path. Logging in again from the same scope evicts the old session: when the same user logs in again from the same scope, the old session receives a notice that it has been superseded and is disconnected. When troubleshooting a connection that dropped on another client, first check whether it was the same scope logging in again. Passwords are stored as Argon2 hashes; plaintext never reaches the database. Presence Presence is recorded separately by client type, with the Beehive (web), the Pupa (desktop), and the Helm (cli) as three independent lines; roughly 90 seconds without a touch counts as offline, with a sweep interval of 30 seconds (minimum 10 seconds). As a result, presence in the user list is split into web, desktop, and cli columns — "online" is no longer a yes-or-no value, and to see who is online on which form you look at the matching column. The management exit is at /wunder/admin/gateway/presence. Unit tree At startup, if the unit table is empty, it is automatically seeded from a unit template. The unit tree is at most 4 levels deep. The unit-head role is allowed only on the two paths /wunder/admin/orgunits and /wunder/admin/useraccounts; its data scope equals the units it heads plus their descendant units, and stepping outside that scope is a permission denial. The frontend's check is only a convenience; the unit-head boundary is ultimately enforced by the server. Levels and credits Levels lean toward growth display: XP equals the integer number of seconds the session has run, the level cap is 200 (MAXUSERLEVEL), and the XP needed to reach the next level increases as 240 + 28L + 0.9L². Levels unlock no resource; they only reflect time spent. Credits lean toward governance: every user holds an integer Credits account with a balance, cumulative issuance, cumulative consumption, and a daily grant (1000 per day by default). It is an abstract allowance of issuance and deduction, not a token count — each request sent to the model service deducts exactly 1 Credit, independent of token metering. When the balance is short, a new request is rejected by quota and returns a snapshot of the remaining allowance; administrator accounts are exempt from deduction but still record request counts. Worker cards and threads | Concept | What it is | | --- | --- | | worker card (.worker-card.json) | An agent's portable definition document, holding basic information (identifier, name, description, icon), prompts, capabilities, interaction, runtime settings, and preset publication status | | Thread / session | The continuous unit of execution once an agent is invoked; one agent can hold several independent task threads at once | Sessions bind to an agent by agent id, and their task threads stay independent of one another. After a preset agent is published, you can control which units can see it and decide which fields a bound user may change. Note that the disk directory for preset cards (useragents.workercardsroot) is an empty string by default — without explicit configuration there is no preset card loaded from disk, so this capability does not ship out of the box. Approval mode has three values, suggest, autoedit, and fullauto, with fullauto the default. Data isolation Sessions, tasks, workspaces, tools, and channel bindings are all isolated by user ownership, and the user-facing side checks ownership handler by handler. Cloud files and execution boundaries are carried by a sandbox: read-write and execute operations run in each user's own container, mounting only that user's own directory, and path checking is no longer responsible for tenant isolation. Quotas, levels, and presence are account-level; model configuration and preset agents are unit-level or global-level. Points not to mix up A token is not a self-contained JWT and cannot be parsed offline — it is an opaque random string, verified by a database lookup, and revocation takes effect immediately. A lost refresh cannot be replaced by resending the old one; replaying an old refresh triggers whole-family revocation, and the correct move is to log in again. Credits are not a token budget; they are an integer request allowance, one deduction per model request, with token usage metered separately. A unit head cannot manage every admin page; it is allowed only on the unit and user-account paths, and only within descendant units. A worker card is not a task thread; it is an agent's definition document, while a thread is a unit of execution — two different layers. The system does not ship a set of preset agent cards; the preset card directory is empty by default, and nothing exists until it is configured. Identity checks Tokens Presence Unit tree Levels and credits Worker cards and threads Data isolation Points not to mix up

title: Interlink
summary: Device management, workspace access, and thread control after a local workbench signs in to the cloud.
text: Interlink Device management, workspace access, and thread control after a local workbench signs in to the cloud. Pupa remains a local AI workbench that works offline. After it signs in to the Hull, it can use cloud agents and threads without opening a local port. If the user explicitly enables local sharing, Beehive can access the device's authorized workspaces and threads through the Hull. Helm exposes the same operations for manual and scripted use. Sign-in and sharing The first Pupa or Helm sign-in creates an independent device session. It does not automatically expose local files or threads. The user can select off, summary sharing, or full sharing in account settings, and Bridge policy can further restrict every device. “Signed in”, “tunnel online”, and “this operation is authorized” are separate states. Sign-in permits cloud access; an online tunnel is required to operate a local device; mutations and execution also require capability, policy, and approval checks. Prerequisites 1. Pupa or Helm is signed in to the Hull. 2. To access a local device, that device is online and its owner enabled sharing. 3. The Hull is the authority for accounts, devices, quota, and policy. Capabilities | ID | Capability | What it means | |------|------|------| | R1 | Device state | The Hull distinguishes a valid sign-in, a live tunnel, and effective capabilities; it presents online / away / busy / reconnecting / offline | | R2 | Workspace visibility | The local workspace appears in the Beehive as a shadow projection, projecting metadata summaries (thread directory, directory-tree summary, scheduled tasks, usage); file contents are not mirrored, and are pulled on demand over the interlink tunnel as the user acts | | R3 | Cloud controlling local | The Beehive can issue graded operations to online local nodes (query / session control / workspace write / tool execution); sensitive operations go through local human-in-the-loop approval, and everything is audited | | R4 | Local controlling cloud | The Pupa and the Helm treat the cloud as a symmetric node — browse the cloud workspace, send messages to cloud threads, read thread event streams; the Helm provides a scriptable command group | The unified state model: | State | Meaning | |------|------| | online | Online and idle | | busy | Online and executing | | away | Online but inactive | | reconnecting | Recovering from a dropped connection | | offline | Offline | Entry Points Pupa | Entry point | What it does | |------|------| | Account settings | Sign-in state, local sharing permission, and sharing level | | Cloud agents and threads | Agents, recent threads, send, stop, tool approval, live status, history pages, and full-text copy | | Local approval | Controlled requests from Beehive to this machine | Beehive (web) | Entry point | What it does | |------|------| | Sidebar | Local workspaces sit beside the cloud workspace: the default root is “device name-Local workspace”, named roots are “device name-workspace name”, and selecting one expands that workspace’s local threads beneath it | | The "cloud / device" dropdown switcher | Removed | Helm | Entry point | What it does | |------|------| | The cloud subcommand group | devices / ws / threads / thread / send / watch / audit / approve | | cloud status | Combines four sections: interlink tunnel, pending approvals, other devices, cloud workspace usage | | cloud watch | Frame types are snapshot / delta / command / error / close | Security Boundary | Boundary | Meaning | |------|------| | No public inbound entry point | Reverse tunnel: the local side only makes outbound connections, opens no listening port, and control traffic is delivered over the already-established link | | Least capability | Each class of remote operation is a declarative capability, read-only by default | | Explicit authorization | Write and execution classes require local user authorization, and an administrator can tighten it further in the Bridge | | Graded approval | Risk tiers L0–L3, see the table below | | Complete audit | Every remote operation forms a chain that can be inspected | | One-click shutdown | The kill switch is held by the user | Risk tiers: | Level | Operations covered | Approval | |------|------|------| | L0 read-only | node.summary / shadow.refresh / workspace.list\|search\|stat\|read / threads.list\|get | No approval needed | | L0+ | workspace.read:binary | No approval needed + audited | | L1 session | thread.create / thread.message / thread.cancel / thread.answer | Local-device operations normally need local approval; a user's own cloud threads use account authorization | | L2 workspace write | workspace.write\|mkdir\|move\|copy\|delete | Approval mandatory, cannot be lowered | | L3 execution | tool.exec (allow-listed commands) / agent.spawn | Approval mandatory + disabled for administrators by default, can be enabled | L3 is off by default: tool.exec and agent.spawn are not in a device's capability set by default; approvals are never remembered; only a summary of the execution result is returned. L2 writes are backed up first: write operations are backed up to 工作区/.interlinkbackup/ / (the most recent 50 generations are kept), and the result reports the SHA256 before and after. Constraints Disconnection and recovery The Pupa reconnects with backoff. While the Hull process remains running, its bounded queue retains commands that have not been sent and delivers them after reconnection. Commands already sent, executing, or awaiting approval on the device fail explicitly when their connection ends, avoiding duplicate operations. After a Hull restart, unfinished commands are settled in bounded batches with SERVERRESTARTED. Command bodies are not persisted, so arguments are never reconstructed from digests and writes are not replayed automatically. Queries can be submitted again; check the actual outcome of a write before resubmitting it through the normal approval flow. Remote thread views obtain a new snapshot after reconnecting. Boundaries Local and cloud threads are not merged. Interlink is remote operation, not data synchronization. No full mirroring or two-way synchronization of workspace files — only metadata projection plus on-demand pull. No graphical remote control; control granularity stops at the engine and file APIs. No NAT hole-punching; all traffic is relayed through the Hull. The Pupa and the Helm do not interlink directly; local-to-local access always goes through the Hull. Remote file reads use a 256 KiB inline-result boundary; larger device files use bounded chunks. Cloud-direct execution has no device data channel, so larger reads and writes must be split. Beehive does not offer binary upload, archive, or batch file operations. Sign-in and sharing Prerequisites Capabilities Entry Points Pupa Beehive (web) Helm Security Boundary Constraints Disconnection and recovery Boundaries

title: Architecture
summary: One core and engine shared by the four forms, the fixed path a message takes inside a session, storage choices, bounded views, external interfaces, and runtime defaults.
text: Architecture One core and engine shared by the four forms, the fixed path a message takes inside a session, storage choices, bounded views, external interfaces, and runtime defaults. All four forms share the same core and engine, differing only at the access layer. Real execution happens inside sessions, and the interface reads a bounded display view that is paginated and carries a byte budget. Forms and Delivery | Form | How it is delivered | Interface | | --- | --- | --- | | Pupa | A desktop app; the engine ships inside the local process and calls in-process by default without local HTTP | Native UI, compiled into the app | | Beehive | A web app; its build artifacts are served read-only by a separate web service, not hosted by the Hull itself | Single-page app | | Helm | A command-line program; when terminal conditions are not met it degrades to one-shot execution instead of the full-screen interactive interface | Terminal UI | | Hull | A server process, mounting Bridge and a few static directories | Bridge (no build step) | Message Path From the moment you send a message to the moment the final reply is stored, the order is fixed: | Step | What it does | | --- | --- | | Access | The main chat channel takes the request and can submit, resume, observe, cancel, and approve it | | Admission | The session runtime decides whether to run it immediately or queue it — the single decision point for "dispatch or queue" | | Record the user round | A user round is allocated idempotently; this is the only write entry for the session record | | Prepare the request | Context, visible tools, and the system prompt are assembled, and a decision is made on whether to freeze | | Main loop | Every model call increments the model round by one | | Run tools | Policy and approval, hooks, timeouts, and budget come first, then the call is dispatched to the actual tool | | Final reply | Multiple refreshes within the same model round update the same visible output item and never append duplicate bubbles | | Real-time push | Emitting an event writes to the persistence layer synchronously, and subscribers are notified only after the write completes | Three places that are easy to mislocate: The status registry the interface queries for a session's current state is a different thing from the session runtime that actually runs execution. In-process wake signals only exist to accelerate; across multiple instances, correctness comes from polling convergence, not from them. The four phases of a tool — pre, execute, post, result — are only a descriptive model; hooks are off by default and are not part of the execution main chain. Data and Storage Storage is split by purpose: thread logs, sessions, workspaces, memory fragments, and so on each form their own group, and the engine depends only on this set of interfaces without caring which database sits underneath. For the choice of database: with no configuration it is SQLite, and configured as PostgreSQL it runs on PostgreSQL. There is no version table and no migration-script directory. Tables are created idempotently on startup and new columns are detected at startup, so there is no such thing as migrating by version number. Every kind of record — sessions, round tails, workspaces, media attachments, memory fragments, knowledge vectors, users and quotas, channel bindings, interop shadows — is defined together. Bounded Views What you see is a bounded display view, not a full history you can page through to the end, and not a complete snapshot of execution. | View | Per page | Cap | Response budget | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Chat page (one row per user round) | 12 | 20 | 128 KB | | Thread trace page (per entry) | 80 | 100 | 192 KB | | Body chunks | 8 KB per chunk | — | fetched on demand | The mechanisms that go with it: a write also produces a projection table and a truncated preview; when a projection is not ready it falls back to a bounded window over the source table; background rebuilds stay at no more than 1% duty cycle; and each change push fetches 200 items. The machinery that measures historical usage and budgets for context compression does not handle pagination. External Interfaces | Surface | Fact | | --- | --- | | HTTP | Routes share the /wunder/ prefix, and error responses have exactly one source format | | WebSocket | Six channels: chat, the core request surface, gateway, interop tunnel, interop remote observer, and world / LAN | | Gateway | Not an HTTP gateway, but an access registry plus targeted RPC plus online-presence broadcast; its only transport is /wunder/gateway/ws | | Channels | Adapter registration; a bounded inbound queue, and a persistent outbound outbox with backoff retry | | Interop | Local nodes are outbound-only; one tunnel carries three planes; capabilities are tiered L0–L3, and the default device capability set excludes L3 | | MCP | The Hull has a built-in service endpoint at /wunder/mcp (streamable-http), and external MCP clients are registered in configuration | Runtime Defaults | Item | Default | | --- | --- | | Hull listen | 0.0.0.0:8000, overridable by environment variable or configuration | | Active session cap | 300 (unlimited for administrators) | | Session lock | 120 s timeout, 5 s heartbeat | | Model / tool timeout | 120 s each | | Model round cap | 1000 for non-administrators | Limits "The Beehive page is hosted by the Hull." No. The Hull mounts only Bridge and a few static directories; Beehive's build artifacts are served by a separate web service. "The front end needs several fetches to get the full history." The front end was never meant to get the full history; it consumes a paginated view and fetches body chunks on demand. "Pupa calls its own backend over local HTTP." By default it is a native in-process call; the standalone compatibility bridge is kept only for existing clients. "Swarm orchestration is still part of the architecture." The engine and scheduling surface no longer have this module; only an empty directory remains, and session write permission is always writable. Forms and Delivery Message Path Data and Storage Bounded Views External Interfaces Runtime Defaults Limits

title: Agent Loop
summary: The model-round granularity of the main loop, round and tool-call budgets, circuit-breaking and timeout guardrails, and the frozen system prompt of a thread.
text: Agent Loop The model-round granularity of the main loop, round and tool-call budgets, circuit-breaking and timeout guardrails, and the frozen system prompt of a thread. The engine calls the model repeatedly to advance a task, and each model call can carry a batch of tool executions, until it produces a deliverable result or hits a brake. The goal is stated once; the steps in between need no steering. Main loop Each model round does three things: it checks whether it should yield and whether the round cap has been exceeded, compressing the context when necessary; it calls the model and gets back a piece of text or a batch of tool calls; and it runs those tool calls in parallel or exclusively, writing the results back into the history as observations before moving to the next round. When there are no tool calls, or a brake is hit, the round lands and the loop exits. The granularity follows Sessions and Rounds: One model round is one model call by the engine. A single round can contain several tool calls, and tool calls are not counted as separate rounds. Each round corresponds to one visible output in the interface; a tool batch is a separate entry in the timeline but is not a separate round. Guardrails Model round cap: non-administrator accounts default to at most 1000 rounds, and it stops once they are used up. Per-round tool-call budget: at most 10000 tool calls in a round; memory recall 2000 and library-query calls 2000 (relaxable to 10000 when necessary), and calls of a type beyond its limit are rejected. Repeated-failure circuit breaker: it stops when the same failure fingerprint recurs — 5 times for non-retryable errors, 2 times for parameter or protocol errors, and 4 times for "succeeded without progress"; after stopping it relays the failure reason to you. Context-overflow self-healing: at most 8 recovery attempts, each doing a corrective compression first and then retrying. Empty-output protection: one automatic retry (resampling with reasoning effort turned off); if it is still empty, it errors out and stops. Timeouts: model and tools default to 120 s each, with an additional idle watchdog; a timeout counts as a failure toward the circuit breaker. Session lock: the same thread runs serially, with a lock TTL of 120 s and a 5 s heartbeat; if the holder exits abnormally, the TTL releases it. Active-session cap: non-administrators are limited to 300, and beyond that requests queue or are told to try again later. Tool parallelism: at most 4; read-only tools run in parallel and exclusive tools run serially. Approval and risk tiering are independent of the loop: write or execute calls suspend and wait for your decision, and approval results are cached by tool category for 600 s so the same kind of operation is not asked about again and again. Terminal states Every round of the loop must finally land on a result, which the interface state reflects: Completed normally: a deliverable reply is produced. Rejected: the request was not admitted (busy, quota exhausted, invalid request). Cancelled: you stopped it yourself. Failed: the execution errored (tool guardrail, no-progress guard, model error). While it waits for your input or for an approval, the thread is not in a terminal state; it is still within its lifetime. Threads An agent can hold several independent task threads at once; scheduling, locking, and realtime state are all isolated per thread, and different threads do not block one another. Once a thread is set, the system prompt is frozen and long-term memory is injected only once at initialization and never rewritten afterwards. This keeps long tasks behaviorally stable and lets the model-side cache be reused. A subagent is a unit of work the main agent creates on the fly; it runs its own loop, passes results back to the parent thread, and is reclaimed when the task ends. This is the only form of collaboration. Intervention An approval pops up, so approve or reject it, and the thread continues. The inquiry panel asks, and the thread moves to waiting for human input; after you add an instruction, the new user round carries the new context. Seeing "running tool" or several tool entries appearing one after another means the loop is advancing. Sending the same sentence again does not speed it up; it only queues another user round. There has been no output for a long time while the state is still running, so stop the thread and restate the goal. Open a new thread when the topic changes, the context is already very long, or you need a clean prompt base: after an agent's setup or its memory is changed, only a new thread picks it up. Points not to mix up The claim that every tool call counts as a round is wrong — a tool batch belongs to the same model round. The loop does not retry without limit; repeated failures, progress-free successes, overruns, and empty output all have circuit breakers. A still interface does not mean the loop has stopped; waiting for approval, waiting for input, and queued are all still within the lifetime. Streaming output is only a way of presenting things; the truth of the loop is in the thread ledger — see Streaming Execution. A subagent does not share the parent thread's context; it is an independent thread with an independent loop, interacting only through callbacks and a mailbox. Main loop Guardrails Terminal states Threads Intervention Points not to mix up

title: Tools
summary: How the four layers — tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools — are told apart, canonical names and aliases, dispatch order for dynamic registration, default sets and visibility gates, and the two result-trimming tracks.
text: Tools How the four layers — tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools — are told apart, canonical names and aliases, dispatch order for dynamic registration, default sets and visibility gates, and the two result-trimming tracks. The agent's ability to act is collectively called "tools," but tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools are four different layers, and conflating them is the most common cause of broken configuration. Tools layer diagram: tool description, execution layer, model input results, and display projection—four related layers The four layers | Layer | What it is | Who uses it | How to tell | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Tool | Executor: one call reads a file, runs a command, or sends a request | The model calls it directly; the engine dispatches and runs it | Registered in the tool catalog and carries a dispatch branch | | Skill | Knowledge-and-script package: a directory holding the SKILL.md body and an entry script | The model can call it by skill name, or read the body through the skill-call action | Registered in the skill catalog | | Capability | Selection unit on the governance side: a unified descriptor an administrator uses to choose what an agent may use | Configured on the admin side; never enters the execution chain | Its source is built-in, MCP, skill, knowledge base, user MCP, user skill, user knowledge base, or shared | | User tool | An extension the user connects, in three kinds: MCP, skill, knowledge base | Mounted per user; the alias enters the routing table | Registered in the user tool catalog | A capability being selected does not mean an executor exists, and an executor existing does not mean the model can see it. Canonical names and aliases Most of the tool names the model sees are Chinese canonical names, with English aliases alongside, and a normalization pass runs before every invocation. | Canonical | Common aliases | Canonical | Common aliases | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 执行命令 | executecommand | 读取文件 | readfile | | 命令会话 | commandsession, writecommandstdin | 写入文件 | writefile | | ptc | programmatictoolcall | 文本编辑 | edit, patch, applypatch, 应用补丁 | | 列出文件 | listfiles | 搜索内容 | searchcontent | | glob | — | 技能调用 | skillcall, skillget | | 计划面板 | updateplan | 问询面板 | questionpanel, askpanel | | 定时任务 | scheduletask | 记忆管理 | memorymanager, memorymanage | | 子智能体控制 | subagentcontrol | 网页抓取 | webfetch | When a tool is written down in configuration, logs, or documentation, give both the canonical name and the alias; writing only one makes the two easy to mismatch. Dynamic registration The names that enter the model's tool list are assembled from four kinds of dynamic registration. | Source | Name on the model side | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | MCP server | server@tool | Registered tool by tool; on a name clash the display name gains a server-name or hash suffix | | Packed MCP | server@mcppack | A server marked as packed folds into a single tool whose actions are list, get, and call | | Skill | The skill name itself | A skill name can be called directly; the skill-call action reads the body and substitutes the skill root-path placeholder | | Knowledge base | The knowledge base name | Registered one base at a time, replacing the old single knowledge tool | | User-tool alias | The alias | Dispatch routes by alias first; a hit goes straight to the user tool | Dispatch order is alias → skill → MCP → knowledge base → built-in tools, and a hit earlier in the chain short-circuits the rest. Default sets and per-form differences Default tool sets, the desktop hidden set, and the desktop extra set all have a single registration; do not keep a second copy in the docs or the configuration. | Set | Contents | | --- | --- | | Default built-ins (13) | 定时任务, 记忆管理, 执行命令, 命令会话, ptc, 列出文件, glob, 搜索内容, 读取文件, 网页抓取, 技能调用, 写入文件, 文本编辑 | | Default skill | 技能创建器 | | Desktop hidden (neither selectable nor on by default) | getgoal, creategoal, updategoal (injected automatically by the runtime per session), 会话线程控制, 会话让出 | | Desktop extras, on by default | 读图工具, 桌面控制, 子智能体控制 | 网页搜索 and ptc are temporarily withdrawn, not deleted: the code is kept and dispatch still recognizes them, but the availability check returns unavailable for both, so neither the model nor the user can see them. To restore them, remove the matching entries from the withdrawal list. Visibility also runs through a few real gates. | Gate | Effect | | --- | --- | | The model has no vision | Filters out 读图工具 and the desktop tools | | The matching model or service is not configured | Speech generation, speech-to-text, image generation, and video generation each go unavailable | | Configuration not enabled | 网页抓取, 网页搜索, the 17 native browser tools, and the desktop tools | | Form | The desktop form filters out the hidden set | Browser is not a single tool: once enabled it registers 17 native tools named browser, and the aggregate display name "Browser" is only a documentation convention. Result trimming Display trimming and model-input trimming are separate and do not affect each other. | Track | Rule | Affects | | --- | --- | --- | | Display | A preview of at most 2,400 characters or 16 lines, with an ellipsis past that | Only the client display; the raw result is kept in full and can be copied | | Model input | Trimmed by budget, with reproducible old observations compressed | What the model sees at the next step | Seeing "…" in the UI does not mean the model sees that same truncated copy; and when the model's context has been compressed to a preview, the UI may still show the full content. To judge context pressure, look at the compression page and the usage page, not the collapsing in the UI. Approval tiers Approvals are filed by the tool's risk category, and there are four categories: read-only, file write, running a command or a script, and controlling host capabilities. Pending requests are registered in two kinds by source: chat connection and channel. The cache that lets one approval cover a short window lasts 600 seconds within the same session. Execution policy has three states: allow, audit, and enforce; under enforce, high-risk actions must have human approval. A front-end confirmation cannot replace back-end authorization. The four layers Canonical names and aliases Dynamic registration Default sets and per-form differences Result trimming Approval tiers

title: Tool System
summary: The path a tool call takes from parsing, orchestration, and dispatch to persistence, reasons a tool is invisible, naming and registration, parallelism, timeouts, budgets, clipping, and MCP integration.
text: Tool System The path a tool call takes from parsing, orchestration, and dispatch to persistence, reasons a tool is invisible, naming and registration, parallelism, timeouts, budgets, clipping, and MCP integration. Layered concepts, the default set, and naming conventions live in Tools (core concepts), and per-tool usage is in the Tools overview. Call Path Two points are easy to get wrong: The four stages "pre → execute → post → result" only describe the model; hooks are off by default and are not the main execution chain. A business failure is not raised as an error in the dispatch layer but returned as a normal path. "The tool returned but the business did not succeed" is normal, and the model reads the reason for the failure. Why a Tool Is Invisible | Where it is stuck | Criterion | | --- | --- | | Not registered | The name is not in the canonical-name / alias table, and no matching MCP, skill, or knowledge base exists | | Temporarily withdrawn | Web search and ptc: the code is still there but they are invisible in every case | | Not in the capability selection layer | The administrator has not selected that capability for this agent | | Filtered by form | Desktop mode hides target-management actions and session thread control / session yield | | Filtered by a capability threshold | Without vision, image reading and desktop tools are filtered out; the multimodal set needs a matching model; web fetching / browser need configuration enabled first | | Name short-circuited | When an alias and a skill share a name, the earlier route matches first | Naming and Dynamic Registration MCP tools are named "server @ tool"; a package-enabled server folds into a single tool operated through three actions: list, get detail, and call. When a tool name collides across servers, a server-name segment is appended; a collision within one server adds a runtime suffix. A skill name can be called directly; a knowledge base is registered library by library, and there is no single "knowledge base" tool. A user-defined tool alias enters the alias table and is routed by alias first during dispatch. Parallelism, Timeouts, and Budgets | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Parallelism ceiling | 4 | | Parallel decision | Whether a batch of tool calls can run in parallel is decided in the orchestration layer | | Lock semantics | A parallelizable tool takes a read lock; an exclusive tool takes a write lock | | Default tool timeout | 120 seconds (minimum 1 second) | | Tool-call budget | 10000 per round | | Memory-recall budget | 2000 per round | Tools outside the parallelism allowlist run serially, deliberately: write and execution tools are exclusive. Two Clipping Channels for Results | Channel | Behavior | Impact | | --- | --- | --- | | Display | Preview 2400 characters and 16 lines, with an ellipsis beyond that | Affects client rendering only; the original message and copied content stay complete | | Model input | Truncate head and tail by budget; older reproducible observations go to micro-compaction | Decides what the model sees next | The budget into the model: 10000 characters at each of head and tail; arrays at most 128 items (48 head + 16 tail); paged results 500 items (180 head + 60 tail). Clipping adds a "truncated" marker, so the model can see that content was cut. Micro-compaction conventions: keep the most recent 5 groups, collapse older observations into a 768-byte preview, and only act when at least 256 tokens are saved. MCP Integration An external MCP client must be configured with a name, endpoint, transport, request headers, authentication, allowed tools, whether to package, and tool specs. The hull's built-in MCP service endpoint is /wunder/mcp (streamable-http), exposing two tools, wunder@excute and doc2md; it returns 501 when the matching capability is off. The standalone Python FastMCP service carries its own configuration and toolset and is not part of this engine. Protocol and Provider The tool-call protocol is decided by the provider: | Situation | Mode | | --- | --- | | The model explicitly configures a tool-call mode | Follow the configuration | | The provider is openai | Text-protocol tool calls | | Any other provider | Native function calls | | An unrecognized value | Fall back to the tag / xml text protocol | The text protocol's lark syntax is currently reserved for the patch form of text editing; parameter repair and nested restoration happen in the core library. There is no separate tool-protocol branch for Win7; the confirmed difference is only on the interop side — an older Win7 node does not declare the "execute command" capability. Removed and Merged | Status | Item | | --- | --- | | Removed | User-world tools, channel tools, a2a tools, finalresponse, a2ui tools, LSP query / node-call tools, and the standalone sleep-and-wait tool | | Merged | applypatch merged into text editing (one tool with three forms: replace / patch / subcommand) | | Semantics changed | Session yield replaces the old sleep-and-wait | | Temporarily withdrawn | Web search and ptc (code kept, invisible) | Limits The four-stage model is not the main execution chain, and hooks are off by default. A clipped result does not mean the model cannot see it: the display channel and the model input channel are separate. More tools do not mean better selection; many names and vague descriptions raise the error rate, so the default set is deliberately restrained. A tool error is not a failed call: a business failure is returned to the model as a normal result with a reason and a next-step hint. Only reads on the parallelism allowlist can run in parallel; writes and executions are exclusive. Win7 has no tool-protocol fallback branch. Call Path Why a Tool Is Invisible Naming and Dynamic Registration Parallelism, Timeouts, and Budgets Two Clipping Channels for Results MCP Integration Protocol and Provider Removed and Merged Limits

title: Realtime
summary: WebSocket endpoints and event categories, cursor-based catch-up after a disconnect, backpressure and slow-client uncoupling on a bounded projection, and interlink as a separate realtime path.
text: Realtime WebSocket endpoints and event categories, cursor-based catch-up after a disconnect, backpressure and slow-client uncoupling on a bounded projection, and interlink as a separate realtime path. Realtime covers three things: the process stays visible, a disconnect can be caught up on, and what the client sees matches backend truth. The approach is durable events, cursor-based catch-up, and a bounded projection — not a full re-pull after a reconnect. Realtime diagram: thread facts projected to client state through event streams and recovery mechanisms Truth and projection The thread log is the single source of truth. Every event push is written synchronously to the persistence layer first, and only then travels the realtime channel. The change wake-up signal only wakes subscribers; it is not a data source, and not the truth. Three things follow directly: A dropped push can be recovered; the truth cannot be lost. When the interface shows something odd, trust the actual execution state — do not decide from the UI whether a task has finished. To tell whether a turn has ended, look only at terminal events, not at "it seems to have gone quiet". WebSocket endpoints Streaming chat output runs only over WebSocket. Requesting the chat stream over HTTP is rejected with a message pointing you to /wunder/chat/ws. SSE is for external workflows only and is not a fallback for chat. Endpoints are distributed by purpose: | Endpoint | Purpose | | --- | --- | | /wunder/chat/ws | Main channel for the thread runtime: connect, heartbeat, start, resume, subscribe, and cancel, plus goal-type and approval-type messages | | /wunder/ws | Core request surface: request submission and streaming responses | | /wunder/gateway/ws | The gateway's three roles (operator, node, channel): request/response/event/heartbeat | | /wunder/interlink/ws (paired with POST /wunder/interlink/channelticket) | Local node reverse tunnel | | /wunder/interlink/remotews | A browser observing a remote single thread; forwarding only, nothing persisted | | /wunder/userworld/ws, /wunder/desktop/lan/ws | Subscribing to and sending world-session messages; LAN networking | Handshake and authentication: send a connection envelope first, or pass accesstoken / token directly as a query parameter. Any other message before the handshake completes is rejected. Events Event names are not enumerated in one place — each is declared where it is sent, and a new one is added the same way. The events that currently exist fall into these categories by purpose: | Category | Events | | --- | --- | | Projection and catch-up | threadviewchange, threadviewrequired, threadsnapshotrequired, threadstatus | | Thread content | threaditemtail, threaditemdelta | | Model output | llmoutputdelta, llmrequest | | Tools | toolcall, toolresult | | Queueing | queueenter, queueupdate, queuestart, queuefinish, queuefail | | Usage and quota | modelrequestusage | | Terminal state | final, turnterminal | | Flow control and errors | heartbeat, slowclient, streamoverflow, error; resumerecommended is emitted together with slowclient or streamoverflow | Catch-up after a disconnect A reconnect does not pull everything again; it catches up with cursors. Three cursors each cover a different span: | Cursor | Meaning | | --- | --- | | changeseq | The thread-change sequence; a request passes afterchangeseq to say where to start catching up | | viewseq | The display-projection sequence; the client uses it to tell whether its local projection is behind | | eventseq / eventid | The sequence number of a single event, sent along with the event | Catch-up goes over HTTP endpoints with the same authentication as the user side: a session's thread-log changes, snapshot, and events (/wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/thread-log/changes|snapshot|events), and the display projection's bootstrap, chat, trajectory, changes, and search (/wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/view/bootstrap|chat|trajectory|changes|search). The consumer always fetches 200 changes at a time and immediately continues to the next page once a page is full. Submission is idempotent: include a clientmessageid, and a repeated submission is simply judged "accepted" and returns the original result. Re-sending the same message after a reconnect does not write it twice. Backpressure and bounds The realtime channel is bounded everywhere; the key values are: | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Per-subscription write queue | 256 | | Slow-client watermark | judged slow when queue remaining ≤ 2 | | Single-fetch cap | 200 | | Heartbeat interval | 15 seconds | | Single message cap | 512 KiB (256 KiB for interlink remote view) | | User input cap | 1,048,576 characters (image attachments not counted) | A slow client is handled by notifying first, then uncoupling: when the write queue crosses the watermark, a slowclient or streamoverflow is sent first along with resumerecommended, and the subscription is then dropped. Better for one lagging subscription to exit and rebuild through catch-up than for a slow client to drag down the whole stream and the engine. The right reaction to a resumerecommended: rebuild the projection through the catch-up endpoints above, then re-subscribe with the new cursor, rather than waiting for the same connection to bring back what was missed. Paged display reads For threads with a lot of data, the timeline and trajectory are not pulled in one shot; they are paged and given a response budget: | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Chat page size / cap | 12 / 20 | | Trajectory page size / cap | 80 / 100 | | Response budget | 128 KB for chat, 192 KB for trajectory | | Body chunking | 8192 bytes | While the projection is not ready, reads fall back to a bounded window over the source table: the page size is clipped to the cap and then to the response budget. Background rebuilds have a duty-cycle cap (no more than 1%, backing off from 5 seconds to 300 seconds after a failure), so a thread that was just imported or heavily changed may still read from the source table for a short while — showing up as a slightly slower first screen, not as missing data. Thread listing pagination caps at 100, and keyword search scans at most 10 pages × 100, that is 1000 entries; anything beyond that is not found. This is a deliberate latency cap. Interlink The realtime surface between local devices (Pupa, Helm) and the cloud is interlink, which differs from the client WebSocket above: Local nodes are outbound-only: they open no listening port. The local side initiates a single long connection, and the control, data, and command planes all share it. Shadow projection: the cloud holds a projection of the local threads and workspace directories. Writes are gated on a live channel; once the channel expires, no new shadow is written. Command ledger and approvals: commands, confirmations, events, and results are all recorded. Risk is tiered L0–L3; tool.exec and agent.spawn are L3, the default device capability set excludes L3, and L3 approvals cannot be remembered. Interlink governance currently exposes only backend interfaces; the Bridge has no interlink panel. Details and protocol are in Interlink. Truth and projection WebSocket endpoints Events Catch-up after a disconnect Backpressure and bounds Paged display reads Interlink

title: Stability
summary: Four kinds of hard constraint — bounded queues, limits and budgets, session locks with a single writer, and circuit-breaker thresholds — plus a uniform error structure and a symptom-to-action table.
headings: Session locks and the single writer
text: Stability Four kinds of hard constraint — bounded queues, limits and budgets, session locks with a single writer, and circuit-breaker thresholds — plus a uniform error structure and a symptom-to-action table. Stability rests on three things: containing the spread (one failing link does not bring down the others), being able to recover (failures have a formal recovery path), and being able to review (errors are structured and classifiable). It comes down to four kinds of hard constraint: bounds, budgets, circuit breaking, and a single writer. Stability diagram: risk sources pass through isolation governance and recovery paths to prevent cascading failures and form a regressable system Bounded queues Every queue has a fixed capacity. A write that fails and times out returns "queue busy" and records a busy metric. There is no unbounded buffer and no silent drop. | Queue | Bound | | --- | --- | | Per-subscription event write queue | 256 | | Slow-client watermark | remaining capacity ≤ 2 | | Single event fetch | 200 | | Thread changes per page | 200 | | Channel ingress | capacity 512 / concurrency 8 / enqueue wait 80 ms | | Workspace write queue | 2048 | Background tasks all start with a tag; a long run raises an alert, and one loop crashing does not take down the process. When troubleshooting, the task tag in the logs tells you which loop it was. Limits and budgets | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | User input cap | 1,048,576 characters; image attachments not counted | | Default model call timeout | 120 seconds | | Default tool timeout | 120 seconds (floor of 1 second) | | Tool concurrency | ≤ 4 | | Turn cap | 1000 by default for non-admins (floor of 2) | | Tool-call budget per turn | 10000 | | Memory-recall budget per turn | 2000 | | Session lock lifetime / heartbeat | 120 seconds / 5 seconds | | Active session cap | 300 by default (constrains non-admins) | | Approval cache | 600 seconds | Session queueing is on by default. With it turned off, sending a message while a run is in progress is immediately judged "user busy" and no queue entry is created either (the Hull warns about this at startup). This is a configuration trade-off, not a failure. Session locks and the single writer The same task thread executes serially, and different threads do not block each other: scheduling, locking, and realtime state are all isolated per thread. A session lock is a persistent lock with a 120-second lifetime, renewed by a heartbeat every 5 seconds. Waiters back off rather than polling on a fixed interval: backoff starts after two attempts, is capped at 3 seconds, and includes jitter; a wait longer than 30 seconds raises an alert. A fixed 0.2-second poll is deliberately avoided here, since a saturated system would otherwise turn its own polling into a storage storm. The single-writer principle: the thread log has exactly one write path. On submission: 1. Each session first passes through a gate that serializes it, so change order matches submission order; 2. The storage call is one short blocking transaction; 3. The cursor is published to the change channel only after the transaction succeeds — the channel carries a wake-up signal, not the truth; 4. Idempotent no-ops (a replayed acceptance, an unchanged state, duplicate feedback) produce no change and no notification; a failed submission never publishes a cursor. Callers must not assemble their own cursors, and must not notify the change channel before the transaction completes. This principle keeps "the order the client sees" consistent with "the order written to storage", and it is what makes lossless catch-up possible after a disconnect. Long-held locks and slow clients are two problems called out for governance: a lock is covered by its lifetime plus heartbeat in case the holder disappears, and a slow client is detected by the watermark, sent a resumerecommended first, and then uncoupled (see Realtime). Recovery and circuit breaking | Scenario | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | Streaming stalls | The idle watchdog judges by how long there has been no activity, not by total elapsed time | | The model returns empty or unusable output | Retried once with thinking off; if it still fails, an output error is reported | | Context over its limit | Progressive compression (triggered at three points: history, overflow, and pre-sampling); overflow recovery at most 8 times | | The same kind of failure recurring | Circuit broken by failure fingerprint | | Network or subscription disconnect | Cursor catch-up, without replaying the whole history | Retry circuit breaking counts by the same fingerprint; the thresholds are: | Condition | Threshold | | --- | --- | | Non-retryable failure | 5 times | | Parameter or structure failure | 2 times (a deterministic error will not improve by waiting, so after two it gives a hint to change course) | | Retryable failure / the same tool failing repeatedly | 5 times | | Successes without progress | 4 times | A fingerprint keeps at most 240 characters of detail. Circuit breaking looks at how many times the same problem repeats, not at how many calls were made in total, so a ten-thousand-call tool budget will not be burned away by a single infinite loop. Error structure Every interface error uses the same structure: it marks the failure and carries an error code, a description for the user, the corresponding HTTP status, an actionable hint, and a trace id and timestamp for tracking, with the trace id and error code also written back in the response headers. Judge by the error code, not by the message text — message text changes with language and version, whereas the mapping between error code and HTTP status is the contract. Symptoms and actions | What you see | What the system is doing | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | Shows compacting or queued | Normal processing | Wait | | slowclient or resumerecommended appears | The subscription was uncoupled to protect the stream | Rebuild the projection through the catch-up endpoints | | Judged "user busy" | That task thread is still executing (the session lock is held) | Queue, or yield/cancel that thread | | Stopped after the same tool failed repeatedly | Fingerprint circuit breaking has tripped | Change the parameters or the path; resubmitting is useless | | Reports an output error | The one-time recovery has been used up | Change the model configuration or rephrase | | Reports insufficient quota | The admission-stage deduction did not pass | See Quota and Token Usage | | The UI and backend state disagree | The projection is behind | Refresh or re-enter; if it still disagrees, look at the runtime state | | You need to start completely over | — | Use "reset work state" (cancels the user's sessions and tasks, clears the workspace, and returns a brand-new session) | Bounded queues Limits and budgets Session locks and the single writer Recovery and circuit breaking Error structure Symptoms and actions

title: Observability
summary: What logs, runtime metrics and alerts, monitoring and thread traces, and performance testing each cover, and the troubleshooting flow that starts from the structured error.
text: Observability What logs, runtime metrics and alerts, monitoring and thread traces, and performance testing each cover, and the troubleshooting flow that starts from the structured error. The clues are concentrated in four places: logs record what happened, runtime metrics and alerts show how loaded the system is right now, monitoring and thread traces reconstruct what a particular thread went through, and performance testing tells you how much the system can take. The four are independent and each covers its own area. Observability diagram: three-layer separation of fact layer, replay layer, and profile layer Logs Logs go to two channels at once: a colorized layer on the console and a file layer with one JSON object per line. Files roll daily, their names begin with server.jsonl, and by default they sit under ./config/data/logs/server. The default level is info, and it can be overridden with the RUSTLOG environment variable; noise from third-party libraries is quieted by default. Retention defaults to 0, which means files are never cleaned up automatically — the system only deletes old files by day once you set an explicit positive number of days. Long-running deployments should either set retention explicitly or rotate the log directory themselves. Note that in sandbox mode nothing is written to files, and only console output is produced.
