The Helm (cli) logs at warn and above by default, the standalone local bridge at info/warn, and neither writes log files. Runtime metrics and alerts The admin side exposes a runtime metrics snapshot with fixed categories: blocking pools are split by database, file, CPU, and external call, each reporting call counts, queue waits, and timeouts; bounded queues report backlog and busy rejections; long-running background tasks report their running counts and any alerts; and the scheduling loop reports whether its heartbeat has stalled. Alerts carry a threshold and a severity. For a given blocking pool, timeout-class alerts (critical) are evaluated before latency-class ones (warning), so when you see a latency warning, first confirm there is no timeout still in queueing or execution. WebSocket and channel event logs WebSocket connections produce structured logs under one target, covering seven stages: open, ready, handshake, handshakeerror, message, parseerror, and close. A connection that will not open, a rejected handshake, or a message that fails to parse can each be told apart by which stage it reached. Channel runtime logs live in an in-memory ring buffer that keeps only the most recent 300 entries; identical content is deduplicated inside a 20-second flood window, nothing is written to the database, and a process restart clears the buffer. They can be queried two ways: the user side reads a user's own channel logs (/wunder/channels/runtimelogs, with /probe for an active probe and /wunder/channels/reconnect for a reconnect), and the admin side reads all of them (/wunder/admin/channels/runtimelogs, which also supports /probe). Use a probe for active connectivity and a reconnect for long-connection failures. Anything that needs long-term auditing has to be shipped to an external log system. Monitoring and thread traces Admin-side monitoring is the entry point to governance views. Sessions are labeled by status — running, waiting, queued, finished, error, cancelling, and cancelled — and you can export a session's thread log, page through its turns, or pull a snapshot (for example, /wunder/admin/monitor/{sessionid}/thread-log/export|turns|snapshot|changes). The log pane on the right side of the Bridge debug panel is the thread trace view; following a single thread's execution record starts there. Not everything has a Bridge panel: interlink governance, long-term memory, and goals are backend-only, with no Bridge UI, so those are checked through their APIs and the logs. Performance entry points | Entry point | What it is for | Key limits | | --- | --- | --- | | Throughput | Stressing the model's streaming capacity, as concurrency × input/output tokens | Concurrency ≤ 1024; input presets 1024…1,048,576 and output presets 1024…8192, with hard caps of 16,777,216 input and 1,048,576 output; 50 runs of history retained | | Performance sampling | A health check in a real environment, sampling commands, IO, and so on | Uses one fixed administrator sampling user; data lands in the workspace at .wunderperf; a single command times out after 5 seconds | | Thread rendering stress test | Generating a large volume of round data to test front-end rendering and projection | User rounds ≤ 2000 and model rounds ≤ 2000, total entries ≤ 6,000,000; concurrent tracking jobs ≤ 8; generation timeout capped at 1 hour | Throughput and performance sampling belong to the admin side (/wunder/admin/throughput/, /wunder/admin/performance/sample). Throughput's live viewing channel (/wunder/throughput/ws) is deliberately exempt from the admin gate and is guarded instead by a single-use ticket. The thread rendering stress test deliberately sits on the user side (POST /wunder/chat/stress-threads) so it can be called with ordinary user credentials for self-testing, but a single job's data ceiling is very high, so watch for pressure under heavy load. The three differ in target and in what they measure — network and model pressure, environment sampling, and front-end data volume — so they should not be treated as one and the same panel. How performance is scored The three forms — the Pupa, the Beehive, and the Hull — are each scored independently on a weighted 0–100 scale, and scores cannot be added across forms. Comparisons are always made in the same environment, through the same entry point, before and after a change; the matching baselines live in the documentation's performance-baseline section. Numbers obtained on a different machine or through a different entry point are not comparable. Troubleshooting flow 1. Get the structured error. When an interface fails, it returns one error object carrying an error code, a description, the HTTP status, an actionable hint for the user, and this request's trace id and timestamp; the trace id and error code are also written back in the response headers. Note the trace id first. 2. Check monitoring. Look at a session's status and turns; when a thread seems stuck, first tell apart "waiting for a person" from "queueing or waiting on a lock". 3. Match it against the logs. Search the log files by trace id; for live-connection problems, filter on the WebSocket stages; for a channel that is not getting through, check the runtime logs and the probe result. 4. Go into the trace. In the thread trace view, check each round's model calls, tool batches, and results to find the first point of divergence. Logs Runtime metrics and alerts WebSocket and channel event logs Monitoring and thread traces Performance entry points How performance is scored Troubleshooting flow

title: Workspaces and the Working Directory
summary: One workspace per user isolation policy, location and the three firm rules on the Pupa and the Hull, file operations, usage statistics, and the local boundary.
text: Workspaces and the Working Directory One workspace per user isolation policy, location and the three firm rules on the Pupa and the Hull, file operations, usage statistics, and the local boundary. A user has exactly one workspace, and the agent's file tools are rooted at it. On the Pupa it is a persistent directory on your machine; on a Hull deployment it is a single per-user directory under the server data root. Isolation Policy Isolation has exactly one layer: per user. Files of different users are fully isolated; neither side can see the other. A user has exactly one workspace; there is no second "personal files / agent files" layer. User, agent instance, and workspace map one to one: one user, one agent, one workspace. Location | Form | Location | How to access | | --- | --- | --- | | Pupa (default) | A persistent directory on your machine | Browse with your system file manager; the agent reads and writes directly | | Hull | A single per-user directory under the server data root | Upload, download, and edit through the "Working directory" area in the Pupa's left sidebar | Three firm rules: | Rule | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Unique | Each user has exactly one workspace at a time; no second directory is opened for another agent | | Fixed | Once assigned it is fixed; a user cannot add, delete, or replace it | | Relative paths | Paths shown in the interface and exchanged through APIs are always workspace-relative; absolute paths are never exposed | What It Carries Data isolation: a user can only access their own workspace; path checks use the user root as the boundary, and out-of-bounds reads and writes are rejected; the agent's file tools are rooted at this directory and no second root is derived. File persistence: the workspace is not cleaned automatically, so the files put in and the files the agent generates are kept long term. Long-lived files go in the workspace and transient transfers in the temporary directory. Root of configuration: the workspace is also the root of "what the agent can see" — the skills directory, knowledge files, and global settings, which the agent reads at startup to initialize. The agent's model, prompts, tools, and approval mode are bound through admin-side presets and managed on the settings page, not by hand-writing files in the workspace. File Operations Access: in the Pupa, use the file manager directly, or the "Working directory" area in the app's left sidebar with its file tree and toolbar. In the Pupa's left sidebar, below the workspace, there is a "Working directory" area with a file tree and an upload / create / refresh / multi-select toolbar. In conversation: hand files to the agent, or have it read and write files in the workspace directly. Reference into chat: pick "Reference into chat" from a file row's menu to bring the file into the input area. Download (Pupa): select files in the tree to download; multi-select bundles them into an archive. File organization: create subdirectories by project or topic, one directory per project, and split source material from output inside it; put files the agent should analyze into the workspace first, then mention the path or filename in the message; the reports and scripts the agent generates land in the same tree. Delete files no longer needed and give files meaningful names. Usage Statistics The bottom of the file area shows used capacity, file count, and directory count. Statistics use bounded traversal and are marked as a lower bound for very large directories. On a Hull deployment with a quota configured, uploads are rejected with a prompt to clean up once the limit is hit; without a quota, only used capacity is shown, with no quota denominator. The Pupa's Local Boundary The Pupa runs locally, and its working directory is a persistent directory on your machine rather than a temporary sandbox: Contents persist and are not periodically cleaned. Whether the agent can access local paths depends on local security settings. It is flexible, but the directory boundaries need checking first. Limits A workspace cannot be moved to another directory, nor can a second one be added. More agents do not mean more working directories: each user has one agent instance and one workspace. Files no longer split into a "personal container" and an "agent container"; that layering is gone, and the user and the agent share the same workspace. The API exchanges paths relative to the workspace root, and absolute paths are not exposed. Isolation Policy Location What It Carries File Operations Usage Statistics The Pupa's Local Boundary Limits

title: Sessions and Rounds
summary: The four-layer numbering of threads, user rounds, model rounds, and entries, plus counting conventions, idempotency and queueing, timeline entries, and interface reading.
text: Sessions and Rounds The four-layer numbering of threads, user rounds, model rounds, and entries, plus counting conventions, idempotency and queueing, timeline entries, and interface reading. The numbering keeps "how many times the user asked" separate from "how many steps the agent took". Statistics, replay, queueing, and token accounting all run on this coordinate system. Structure | Concept | What it is | Decided by | | --- | --- | --- | | Thread / session | The main body of a continuous stretch of execution and dialogue; one session id runs through scheduling, locking, and state | Starting a thread starts a session; a subagent is an independent session traced back by its parent session id | | User round | One accepted human input | Incremented in the session on acceptance; a uniqueness constraint guarantees "one root per round" | | Model round | One model call of the engine's main loop, which may include a batch of tool calls | Incremented once per sample of the main loop | | Entry | The smallest renderable record on the timeline | Upserted by a stable entry id when it is written | The coordinates of the four layers: | Coordinate | Meaning | | --- | --- | | User round | Which user round it belongs to | | Model round | Which model call within that round (empty before sampling begins) | | Round id | The persistent id of that user round, used as the prefix of the entry identifier | | Target round | This round was started by the target driver rather than by a person, so a goal action that needs human authority is not started twice | Counting Conventions One model round = one model call, not "one action". Tool calls belong to a batch within the same model round and are not counted as separate model rounds. One model round produces exactly one visible output item: refreshing several times within the same model round only updates that item and never appends duplicate bubbles. A tool-batch entry on the timeline is not an independent model round. Each tool call is its own entry (merging "in progress → done / failed" by call id), so the number of steps is usually larger than the number of model rounds. A continuation round does not consume a user round: a continuation that carries a root-round reference (for example, the target driver taking over) reuses the same user round and only adds model rounds within it. A user round publishes a change only when it is genuinely newly created; a replayed acceptance is an idempotent no-op that produces no new round and notifies no subscribers. Idempotency and Queueing | Mechanism | Convention | | --- | --- | | Submit idempotency | The same client message id reuses the existing round, so a network retry does not create an extra round | | Serialization within a session | The session lock is isolated per session, with a 120-second timeout and a 5-second heartbeat; an abnormal exit releases it on timeout | | Queueing | The queue toggle is on by default; messages sent while running enter the queue and run in order | | Turning queueing off | A message sent while running is judged "user busy" and not queued (the hull warns at startup), so do not turn it off as a performance tweak | | Background delivery | Scheduled messages take the forced-enqueue path so they are not lost while competing for the lock with human messages | Timeline Entries A session records only events with timeline value: | Entry type | State flow | | --- | --- | | Tool call | In progress → done / failed (merged by the same call id) | | Model call | Numbered by model round | | Visible reply | The output item of that model round | | Approval | Waiting → decided | | Subagent message | Uses the producer-supplied message id as a persistent identity, so a replay never becomes a new entry | | Queue ledger | Pending → running (upserted on the same entry); the interface skips it | Not recorded: transport deltas, heartbeats, progress, context occupancy, workspace updates, model usage, and streaming retries, together with lifecycle receipts (ended, status, model response, and so on — failure details are carried by the round's terminal state). These are visible in the stream but do not become empty timeline entries. Interface Reading The chat page shows one user round per row (12 per page by default, up to 20), folding everything between the final reply into a "working process". The working process is collapsed by default; the first expansion fetches that user round's persistent entries on demand rather than pulling the entire history into the frontend. The entry-by-entry panorama lives in the "thread trace" view (80 per page by default, up to 100), with long bodies fetched in 8 KB chunks. The directory list reads the tail of each round (highest user round, that round's state, a recent-activity summary, and the backfill cursor), querying a page of sessions in one batch. Starting and Reusing Sessions When to start a new session: changing topic; needing to apply new agent settings, a prompt template, or long-term memory (an existing session's prompt is already frozen); or when the context has grown long and is starting to lose early detail. When to keep the current one: the same task is still unfinished, or you need to reference earlier output. Continuing does not recompute the base; it only adds rounds. How to point at "a certain step": give the coordinates "user round + model round", or the entry id directly; for tool batches give the entry sequence number only and do not call it "round N". Common Misreadings "One round = one question and answer" — one user round can contain many model rounds, and each model round can carry a batch of tool calls. "Step count = round count" — they are not equal; steps (entries) are usually more. "A session and a thread are two things" — in this system they are the same: the session is the carrier of the conversation and its records, and the thread is its executing body. "Submitting again charges an extra round" — a retry with the same client message id is idempotent. "A subagent's input shows up in the parent session" — a sub-session's opening user message is hidden by default and skips automatic memory extraction, so it does not pollute your memory. "Token statistics = the provider's bill" — a session records context occupancy (trusting only the value the model reports), not a billing figure. Structure Counting Conventions Idempotency and Queueing Timeline Entries Interface Reading Starting and Reusing Sessions Common Misreadings

title: Streaming Execution
summary: Persist-then-notify channel ordering, the WebSocket channel list, four event classes, cursor-based resumption, and the default bounds.
text: Streaming Execution Persist-then-notify channel ordering, the WebSocket channel list, four event classes, cursor-based resumption, and the default bounds. The execution process reaches the interface in real time, what the interface reads comes from the same source as the session record, and a dropped connection resumes by cursor. Persistence and Notification When the engine emits an event, it first writes it synchronously into the session record (one serial channel per session, a single transaction), and only after the transaction succeeds does it publish the change cursor and wake subscribers. That gives three guarantees: Commit order = change order: each session has its own channel and writes complete in short transactions; a failed commit does not publish a cursor. Idempotent and quiet: a replayed acceptance, an unchanged state, or duplicate feedback produces no change and notifies no one. Waking is only an accelerator: the in-process wake channel is not a correctness guarantee, so the server always keeps a polling fallback for resumption (starting at 250 ms and backing off exponentially to 4 seconds), and multiple instances converge through polling. The text shown in the interface and the text read after a refresh come from the same source; there is no in-between state where the stream has something the store does not. Channels | Channel | Purpose | | --- | --- | | /wunder/chat/ws | The main channel for chat sessions: submit, resume, watch, cancel, and approve | | /wunder/ws | The general request surface (submit one execution and receive it as a stream) | | /wunder/interlink/remotews | A browser watching a single session on a remote device; pure forwarding, not persisted | | /wunder/userworld/ws, /wunder/desktop/lan/ws | In-site sessions and LAN collaboration | The default Pupa form does not go through the local HTTP / WebSocket: an in-process native event channel (bounded at 128 items) delivers directly, and losing a subscription or closing a window does not cancel a round already accepted on the server. ⚠️ Chat has no SSE fallback. The server does provide SSE, but only for the external integration surface and model-proxy calls, not as a degradation channel for chat. Event Classes | Class | Enters the timeline | Usage | | --- | --- | --- | | Entry events (tool call, model call, visible reply, approval, subagent message, compaction, round terminal) | Yes | Upserted by a stable entry id | | Transport deltas (assistant body tail chunk, command output delta) | No | Add characters only: the assistant body uses a tail chunk, command output uses a delta | | Status and receipts (session state, ended, error, session closed, queueing) | Partly (queueing is a persistent record) | Judge the lifecycle; not rendered as entries | | Wake and backfill (view changed, view needs refetching, snapshot needed, stream overflow, slow client, reconnect suggested) | No | The client resumes or refetches wholesale based on these | Statistics (context occupancy, token usage, round usage, model usage, quota) are only for panel refreshes and do not enter the timeline. Disconnection and Backfill The client keeps a persistent cursor (a change sequence number) and sends it when reconnecting: | Situation | Server signal | What the client does | | --- | --- | --- | | Behind, but not by much | Resume sending change rows from the cursor | Apply incrementally in place | | Behind beyond the window | Stream overflow + reconnect suggested | Receive the signal first, then drop that subscription and reconnect by cursor | | The persistent window has been trimmed | Snapshot needed | Give up on resuming and pull one atomic snapshot | | The displayed view is behind | View needs refetching / view changed | Refetch the paged view rather than stitching entry by entry | The backfill interfaces come as a set: session change list, atomic snapshot, event paging, and single-entry body. Default Bounds | Parameter | Value | | --- | --- | | Write queue per connection | 256 (full means slow client) | | Slow-client watermark | 2 (alarm / degrade once the queue is deeper) | | Resume page size | 200 | | Event read limit | 200 | | Heartbeat | 15 seconds | | Single message | 512 KiB (rejected when exceeded; 256 KiB for remote watch) | | Chat page / trace page | 12 (up to 20) / 80 (up to 100), response budget 128 KB / 192 KB | | Body chunk | 8 KB | The frontend consumes a view: a chat page holds only 12 user rounds, and everything between the final reply in each round folds into a "working process" that fetches that round's entries only when expanded. The trace is the entry-by-entry view (up to 8 subagent cards per row). Failure Diagnosis Whether a round is over: look at the round's terminal state (with status, stop reason, and optional error and recovery action) rather than guessing that "it seems stopped". While waiting for approval or more information, the session is still within its lifecycle. Duplicate bubbles: most likely the client appended a new item instead of upserting by entry id. Locate the same item by "round id + model round". Missing characters: check whether the delta was treated as the only source. A delta only provides continuous display; the truth of the body is in the entry, so backfill after reconnecting rather than guessing. Content gets longer after a refresh: a refresh reads the persisted body, which may be more complete than the streamed tail chunk. Limits Streaming and persistence are not two paths: events are persisted synchronously when emitted, and the cursor is published after the transaction. A disconnect is not an interrupted execution: execution continues on the server, and the client simply reconnects by cursor. SSE is not a fallback for chat; chat is WebSocket only. Fetching a few more times will not return the full history: views are deliberately bounded, and moving the full history is exactly what the design avoids. "Seeing text stream out" does not mean "the loop ran many rounds": text deltas and model rounds are two different granularities, and one round can contain thousands of deltas. Persistence and Notification Channels Event Classes Disconnection and Backfill Default Bounds Failure Diagnosis Limits

title: Runtime and Online Status
summary: The six runtime states of a session, interface badges and indicators, how to judge a stuck session, and the sequence for handling inconsistent state.
text: Runtime and Online Status The six runtime states of a session, interface badges and indicators, how to judge a stuck session, and the sequence for handling inconsistent state. Alongside its history, a session maintains a set of runtime states — running, waiting for approval, waiting for your input, interrupting, idle, and not loaded — from which the interface derives a summary snapshot. Session States The first layer is what the session is doing at this moment. | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Running | Actively working | | Waiting for approval | Paused on an action that needs your go-ahead | | Waiting for your input | The agent is waiting for you to add information | | Interrupting | Being interrupted | | Idle | Nothing to do, waiting for your next message | | Not loaded | Not yet loaded into memory | The second layer is a summary snapshot the interface reads directly: whether output is still streaming, whether the session is waiting, whether it is loaded, whether it is active, and whether it has already reached a terminal state. Interface Presentation Session list: the status badges come straight from runtime state — a green dot means an active session, a spinning icon means running, and a waiting icon means waiting for approval or input. Session detail: the status indicator tells you which stage you are at, whether you can send a new message, and whether any approval is pending. Diagnosing a Stuck Session Runtime state is the starting point for troubleshooting. | You want to know | Look at | | --- | --- | | Whether it is still running | Whether output is still streaming | | Whether it is waiting | Whether it is in a waiting state | | Whether it has finished | Whether it has reached a terminal state | | Whether it can still be observed | Whether it is loaded and active | A single coarse running / not-running flag cannot tell "still streaming" apart from "waiting for approval", and it says nothing about whether the session is loaded or has reached a terminal state. Read the full set of snapshot fields. Handling Inconsistent State If the interface and the actual state do not match: 1. Wait a few seconds to see whether it recovers on its own. 2. Refresh the page or restart the app. 3. Use "Reset working state". Limits Waiting for approval is a pause, not an ending — it is still within the session lifecycle. State belongs on the list and event pages too, not only the detail page. The event stream carries the timeline while the runtime snapshot carries the present moment; they are not the same layer. Session States Interface Presentation Diagnosing a Stuck Session Handling Inconsistent State Limits

title: Prompts and Skills
summary: Composition and freezing of the system prompt, the three layers of skills, switching template packs and where changes apply, and the division of responsibility.
text: Prompts and Skills Composition and freezing of the system prompt, the three layers of skills, switching template packs and where changes apply, and the division of responsibility. An agent's behavior is decided by two things: its system prompt (who it is, how it thinks, what principles it holds) and its skills (the concrete method it follows for a class of task). System Prompt The system prompt is the agent's working manual. It sets out the role it plays, the engineering principles it follows, how it uses tools, how it calls on skills, and what memory context it remembers. The system prompt is fixed when the session is created and stays frozen afterward. This keeps the agent's behavior consistent within the same session. Skills A skill is an operating manual for the agent. It bundles a full method, execution scripts, examples and resources, and the constraints and boundaries that apply. When it needs to, the agent reads the complete skill document. A skill packages a method for a class of task, so similar tasks follow the same method. Skills come in three layers. | Layer | Description | Editable | | --- | --- | --- | | Built-in | Shipped with the system | Read-only | | Custom | Created by a user or administrator | Editable | | External | Imported from outside | Depends on the source | Prompt Template Packs wunder supports several prompt template packs: a Chinese pack (Chinese style by default), an English pack (English style by default), and custom packs tailored as needed. To switch, open the agent settings, find "Prompt template", pick one, and save. When it takes effect: a new conversation uses the new template while existing conversations are unchanged. Changing a template and seeing no change in the current conversation is expected; starting a new conversation picks it up. To build a custom template, copy a built-in one, edit the sections (role, principles, additional notes, and so on), and save it to use. Placeholder Resource Paths Resource paths inside a skill document are written as placeholders rather than hard-coded paths. A skill lives in a different actual location in each runtime form, so the system substitutes the correct path when the skill is used. Division of Responsibility | | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Prompt | Defines the long-lived, stable boundary of behavior | | Skill | Defines the additional execution protocol for a class of task | | Memory | Defines the long-term facts injected when a session initializes | The three work together, and their responsibilities are not mixed. Template and Skill Management A template has a clear role, concise principles (keep the important constraints rather than piling them on), no internal contradictions, and is tuned against real results. Skills are managed on the "Tools" page: see installed skills, enable or disable them, create a skill for a particular working scenario, and share one with the team. Combining prompt templates, skills, and models produces agents of different styles: a coding assistant, a copywriter, a data analyst, a translation expert. Limits Changing a template does not affect the current conversation right away; it only affects new conversations. A skill is not just a documentation file; it is a runtime resource the agent can actively read. Memory does not rewrite the prompt every round; it is injected once at initialization. System Prompt Skills Prompt Template Packs Placeholder Resource Paths Division of Responsibility Template and Skill Management Limits

title: Long-term Memory
summary: Injection and freezing rules for structured memory fragments, what memory can hold, initialization injection versus runtime recall, and how it differs from the knowledge base.
headings: Memory and the Knowledge Base Are Not the Same
text: Long-term Memory Injection and freezing rules for structured memory fragments, what memory can hold, initialization injection versus runtime recall, and how it differs from the knowledge base. Memory follows stability over flexibility: it is injected once when the session is created, frozen while running, and supplemented by recall when material is needed. Core Rules 1. Injected once when the session is created: long-term memory is written into the system prompt once, when the conversation starts. 2. Frozen while running: later turns do not change the system prompt. 3. Supplemented by recall when needed: while running, recall adds material, but it does not rewrite the foundation. The reason it is not updated every round: rewriting the system prompt each round would make the agent's behavior unstable (drifting as the conversation goes on), lower the cache hit rate (making it slower), and make problems hard to trace (you could not say what background it was working from at the time). Structure Memory is made of structured fragments, not one long free-form passage. A fragment is found by lookup, replaced without affecting the rest, marked invalid when outdated, and carries traceable version relationships. What Memory Can Hold Who you are: preferences and habits, work background, past decisions. Organizational knowledge: team rules and standards, project background, domain expertise. Personalization: adjusting the answer style to your preferences, referring to your past context, and giving targeted suggestions. Initialization Injection vs Runtime Recall | | Initialization injection | Runtime recall | | --- | --- | --- | | Timing | When the session is created | During the conversation | | How | Written into the system prompt | Added as a tool result | | Effect | Becomes the session's cognitive foundation | Does not rewrite the foundation | | Scope | The life of the whole session | The current round | Managing Memory View: see the current memory in the agent settings. Add: tell the agent "remember this preference," or add it by hand in settings. Delete: remove fragments that are outdated or unneeded. Update: add a new fragment to replace an old one. When it takes effect: a new conversation uses the latest memory at once; an existing conversation is unaffected and keeps using the memory from when it was created. So after updating memory, you need to start a new conversation for it to apply. Memory and the Knowledge Base Are Not the Same | | Memory | Knowledge base | | --- | --- | --- | | Content | Structured personal / organizational facts | Documents, material, and standards | | When used | Injected at initialization | Retrieved while running | | Update frequency | Relatively stable | Can be updated often | | Good for | Preferences, background, decision records | Reference material, technical documents | Limits Memory is not updated every round; it is injected once at initialization. The results of recall are not written back into the system prompt; they are only a temporary supplement. More memory is not better: too much crowds the context and can interfere with judgment. Core Rules Structure What Memory Can Hold Initialization Injection vs Runtime Recall Managing Memory Memory and the Knowledge Base Are Not the Same Limits

title: Quota and Token Usage
summary: How the 1-credit-per-model-request and 1000-per-day grant are issued and deducted, and what the token metrics observe.
text: Quota and Token Usage How the 1-credit-per-model-request and 1000-per-day grant are issued and deducted, and what the token metrics observe. Quota limits how many model requests you can make. Regular users receive 1000 credits per day, the same regardless of organization or level. Unused credits accumulate. The grant is applied once on the day's first use or account adjustment; days when nothing was used are not backfilled. Each real model request costs 1 credit, including the next model call inside a tool loop, compaction summaries, and failed retries. Streaming chunks, standalone tool execution, and history replay cost no credits. A request consumes a credit even if it fails; when the balance is insufficient, no new model request is dispatched. Administrators and unregistered virtual users are not limited by quota. Viewing and Adjusting On the user side, "My Profile" shows the current balance and the daily grant. Administrators can set the balance directly in "User management → Settings", or grant and deduct credits: A value set directly is the final balance after the day's grant is carried over. A grant increases "cumulative granted", while a deduction counts toward "cumulative used"; an operation is rejected when the balance is insufficient. The account shows several numbers: available credits, cumulative granted, cumulative used and administrative deductions, the daily grant, and the most recent grant date. Multiple sessions share one user credit account, and concurrent requests cannot overdraw it. User levels still accumulate experience but no longer award credits. On the first upgrade, an old token-balance account is initialized to 1000 credits and is not converted from its historical token count; a restart afterward does not reset the balance either. Token Observation Token usage describes a model's input, output, reasoning, and context size, and it never affects the credit deduction. A short request and a long request both cost 1 credit. The token metrics you can see include: Context occupancy: the context size most recently observed. The cumulative model tokens consumed within one user request. Model usage events, plus the request count, whether it was charged, the credit consumed in that turn, and the account snapshot for each real model request. In a session, "model request count" and "credit consumption" are two different metrics: for a regular user, one billable model request normally increases each by one; in an exempt case such as an administrator, the request count still increases but credit consumption stays at zero. The account snapshot only shows the balance at that moment and does not represent how much this request deducted. Old credit records are kept only for reading history. Viewing and Adjusting Token Observation

title: Goal Mode
summary: Fields of a session-level persistent goal, the four phases and the continuation gate, the in-process arming flag, model-side operations, and the available entry points.
text: Goal Mode Fields of a session-level persistent goal, the four phases and the continuation gate, the in-process arming flag, model-side operations, and the available entry points. Goal mode hangs a goal on a session and pairs it with a driver that lives only in the current process. Whenever the session goes idle, the driver submits the next continuation (a goal round), and each round spends one unit of the model-round budget; whether it keeps going or stops is decided by the budget, the phase, and whether the goal is blocked. Goal Fields | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Objective | What to do, up to 4,000 characters | | Phase | One of active, paused, blocked, complete — these four and nothing else | | Continuation-round budget (maxgoalrounds) | The most automatic continuations that may run; defaults to 256 when the goal is created | | Started rounds (roundsstarted) | Only ever increases; it is never reset backwards | | Revision | Increments on every change; an update must carry the goal id and its exact current revision, and a mismatch is rejected (compare-and-set on revision) | | Blocked reason | When blocked, a machine code (blockedcode) plus a plain-language explanation (blockedmessage) | When It Applies | Situation | What to do | | --- | --- | | Long tasks with a clear completion condition that the model should push forward over several rounds | Use goal mode | | Something a single round of Q&A can resolve | Just send a message | | Work that needs you in the decision loop often | Talk directly, and add the question panel when needed | | You only want the current round to go deeper | An ordinary round is enough; a model round has no built-in one-step-one-answer limit | Phases | Phase | Meaning | How it is entered | How it is left | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | active | Able to continue | Create a goal, or resume | paused / blocked / complete | | paused | Sitting still; a person can resume at any time | A manual pause, or a continuation round that was interrupted | Resume | | blocked | Automatic continuation stops | The model self-reports the same blocking condition once at least 3 consecutive continuation rounds have run; or the driver fails to enqueue (queue-failed) | Resume (after the blocking condition is resolved) | | complete | Achieved | The model or a person marks it complete, and only when it is truly done | Reopen with a new goal | Whether the next round starts depends on a single gate: the phase is active, the goal is armed inside the process, and roundsstarted has not reached the budget — all three must hold to continue. A person's message always wins; a continuation round never competes with a person for the session. Budget Unit and Round Boundaries The budget is counted in model rounds, not tokens. The system does not track how many tokens a goal burns, there is no token budget, and there is no design in which the budget runs out and drops the goal into some restricted state. There is no cooldown between rounds. As soon as the session is idle, the driver immediately decides whether to send the next round. "Blocked" does not mean "hard": difficulty, uncertainty, and unfinished work are not reasons to report blocked. The agent must name a concrete blocking condition that persists across rounds. Arming Is Not Persisted Whether a goal is armed is an in-process flag and is not stored in the database. After a process restart, a session restore, or a fork, the driver will not pick up automatically even if the phase is still active — it has to be armed again with an explicit updategoal carrying action=resume. When asking why a goal stopped moving, first check whether it is still armed. Model-Side Operations The model side operates on a goal through three built-in tools. | Tool | Effect | | --- | --- | | getgoal | Reads the current goal, including the id and revision that updategoal requires; the authoritative value must be fetched before an update | | creategoal | Infers and creates a goal from a person's direct request; the objective is required and the round budget is optional | | updategoal | Edit / pause / resume / complete / report blocked (action=blocked); needs the goal id plus the current revision, and reporting blocked is rejected before the minimum round count is reached | Authority does not come from anything the model writes: human entry points stamp source = "human" onto the turn and the goal-round driver stamps goalround. Edit, pause, and resume are allowed only in a person's round; complete and report-blocked are additionally allowed in the goal's own automatic continuation rounds. The Pupa (desktop) does not expose these three tools for users to pick (they are hidden built-in capabilities); the runtime injects them per session, and the Beehive (web) and the Helm (cli) reuse the same injection. Entry Points | Entry | Location | | --- | --- | | API | GET/PUT/DELETE /wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/goal (user side; requires an ownership check) | | Slash command | /goal [ \|clear\|edit \|pause\|resume] | | Beehive | A goal bar in the message area | | Pupa | A goal banner above the input box, with inline editing | | Helm | The /goal command | | Bridge | No goal UI (the governance surface offers no goal operations) | Points Often Misread A goal does not stop on a token limit; it looks only at the round budget, the phase, and arming. After a service restart an active goal does not resume on its own; a resume action is needed to arm it again. The model cannot mark a goal blocked at will: the same blocking condition must persist across at least 3 continuation rounds. A goal is not "a tool named goal" but three tools — getgoal, creategoal, updategoal; the old single tool and the old injection marker no longer exist. The Bridge has no goal panel; use the Beehive, the Pupa, or the Helm. Clearing a goal does not undo work already done: messages, tool results, and file changes already stored are kept. Goal Fields When It Applies Phases Budget Unit and Round Boundaries Arming Is Not Persisted Model-Side Operations Entry Points Points Often Misread

title: Companion System
summary: ZIP package and sprite-sheet specification, per-form presentation, scale and position ranges, and user versus administrator permissions.
text: Companion System ZIP package and sprite-sheet specification, per-form presentation, scale and position ranges, and user versus administrator permissions. A companion package is a ZIP holding a manifest and a sprite sheet; at runtime the row played depends on the session state. Companions take no part in execution and do not affect scheduling, so deleting one changes no functionality. Package Structure A companion package is a ZIP that holds exactly two things: a manifest and a sprite-sheet image. The manifest (pet.json) is JSON and states the companion's id, display name, and description, along with where the sprite-sheet file lives. The sprite sheet is a single image whose path the manifest gives. Size limits: the whole ZIP is at most 24 MB, and the single sprite-sheet file is at most 18 MB. Import guards against path traversal inside the archive. Companion files live in one fixed companion directory (config/data/companions/global, overridable through WUNDERCOMPANIONSROOT); embedded forms such as the Pupa and the Helm pin this directory to their own data directory. The directory starts empty, so no companion package ships built in and an empty list is normal. Sprite-Sheet Specification Every frame is a fixed 192 × 208 pixels, and frames of the same state line up horizontally in the same row; one state occupies one row. The row number is the state (rows 0–8): | Row | State | Row | State | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | idle | 5 | failed | | 1 | running-right | 6 | waiting | | 2 | running-left | 7 | running | | 3 | waving | 8 | review | | 4 | jumping | | | The session's runtime state maps to an animation row: running → running (row 7), completed → jumping (row 4), waiting → waiting (row 6), error → failed (row 5), and everything else falls back to idle (row 0). Clicking the companion plays the waving animation once. A companion package may declare fewer rows or frames: out-of-range rows or frames are degraded by a bounds check and never crash. Presentation per Form | Form | Presentation | | --- | --- | | Pupa (Windows) | Native floating window: a Win32 layered window per pet, with dragging and the frame clock on a separate message thread that does not occupy the UI thread | | Pupa (Linux) | No equivalent floating window; the desktop pet exists only on Windows | | Beehive | An in-page overlay that follows the chat state | | Bridge | A companion management panel: upload, edit, delete, and export global companions | | Helm | No companion UI; it only points the companion directory at the local data directory | Scale and Position | Item | Range | | --- | --- | | Stored / menu scale | 0.5–1.6 (presets 0.5 / 0.8 / 1.0 / 1.2 / 1.4 / 1.6) | | Render scale | 0.5–1.8 | | Position | Clamped to the screen work area with margins kept; drag results are saved | The Pupa stores position, per-companion show / scale overrides, and the global message-hint switch in a local file; the Beehive stores them in the browser, so clearing browser data resets position and preferences. Permissions The user side is read-only: four GET endpoints only — the global list, one companion's detail, its sprite sheet, and its exported package (/wunder/companions/global). Adding, changing, and deleting sit on the administrator side (/wunder/admin/companions): list, import, edit and delete, sprite sheet, export package. The import request-body limit matches the ZIP limit, both 24 MB. A "private companion" in the Beehive takes effect only in the current browser and is not uploaded to the server; a global companion is uploaded by an administrator through the Bridge and is then visible to all users. The Bridge is the only upload path. Limits A companion is not another kind of agent; it is only the visual shell of an agent, and one agent binds one companion. Users cannot upload a companion to the server from the Beehive; server-side companions are managed by administrators through the Bridge, and private imports stay in the local browser. The Pupa on Linux has no desktop floating window — the overlay is a Win32 implementation with no Linux equivalent. Companion animation does not affect task execution: the runtime state drives the animation, not the other way around. The system ships no companion package; an administrator uploads them. Package Structure Sprite-Sheet Specification Presentation per Form Scale and Position Permissions Limits

title: Boundary Handling
summary: Graduated compression on context overflow, reconnect and event replay after a disconnect, tool failure handling by type, and queueing with priority.
text: Boundary Handling Graduated compression on context overflow, reconnect and event replay after a disconnect, tool failure handling by type, and queueing with priority. Each failure type has its own path: a failure in one link does not drag the others down, every failure keeps a recovery route, and problems of the same kind can be categorized, reproduced, and verified. Context Overflow As a conversation grows longer and tool results pile up, the total token count approaches the model's ceiling. Compression runs progressively in four levels: | Level | What it does | Loss | | --- | --- | --- | | Level 1 | Remove intermediate tool results | Very low | | Level 2 | Summarize the conversation history | Medium | | Level 3 | Remove earlier parts of the conversation | Higher | | Level 4 | Emergency degradation | Very high | The system prompt never takes part in compression and stays frozen, so compression never changes the agent's behavioral setup. On long conversations, watch context usage and compress proactively with /compact when needed; start a new session once a topic is done. Disconnect and Reconnect After a disconnect caused by network jitter, the interface shows a prompt first and then reconnects automatically with exponential backoff (1 s → 2 s → 4 s → 8 s → 16 s, up to 32 s). Events that were not pushed during the disconnect are cached and replayed once the reconnect succeeds; the interface only prompts for a manual refresh if the replay also fails. When the interface shows "connection lost", wait for the automatic reconnect instead of refreshing repeatedly. Tool Failure | Failure type | Handling | | --- | --- | | Wrong parameters | The agent corrects the parameters itself and retries | | Permission denied | Execution stops and waits for approval | | Temporary error (file locked, network jitter) | Automatic retry | | System error | Limited retry plus degradation | Read the failure notice for the cause and adjust as it suggests (for example, give the correct file path); if it keeps failing, ask an administrator to check the system logs. Oversized Tool Output Three layers of containment: | Layer | Role | | --- | --- | | Execution budget | Caps the size of a single output | | Result trimming | Keeps the head and tail when the limit is exceeded | | Pre-model check | Trims once more before the input reaches the model | A trimmed result tells the agent explicitly that it was cut, so the agent can switch strategy. Queueing and Priority When a conversation is busy, new requests are not turned away but queued and run in turn once it is free. Priority runs from high to low: administrators > high priority > normal > low priority. Limits An agent answering does not mean everything is fine; check whether it stays stable over time and whether it reports failures when they happen. Retrying applies to some error types only. Boundary cases show up often in long conversations and complex tasks. If there is no response for a long time, try cancelling or resetting first; if the state is clearly wrong, use "reset working state"; if it keeps happening, ask an administrator to troubleshoot. Context Overflow Disconnect and Reconnect Tool Failure Oversized Tool Output Queueing and Priority Limits

title: Session Status Guide
summary: When the waiting, thinking, running tools, approval, failed, cancelled, stuck and connection statuses appear, what they mean, and how to handle them.
text: Session Status Guide When the waiting, thinking, running tools, approval, failed, cancelled, stuck and connection statuses appear, what they mean, and how to handle them. During a conversation the interface shows statuses such as thinking, calling a tool, compressing context, or retrying after an error. Status overview The states a conversation passes through from start to finish: Basic statuses | Status | Meaning | When it appears | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Waiting | The request has been submitted and is queued for handling | The system is busy; several requests are running at once | Wait | | Thinking | The agent is analyzing the request and preparing to answer or act | While the model understands the problem and works out a plan | Wait rather than resending the same message | | Running tools | The agent is using tools to carry out the task: reading a file, searching the web, running code | Complex tasks need several tools working together | Watch the progress in the progress area | | Done | The agent has finished and given its final answer | Request handling has ended | Follow up, review the content or files it produced, or start a new task | While tools run, the interface shows prompts such as "Reading file…", "Searching…", and "Running…". Approval statuses | Status | Meaning | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | Approval needed | The agent wants an action that needs confirmation: changing an important file or running a sensitive command; or an approval mode is configured | The interface shows the approval request and a description of the action; click Approve to continue, or Reject to stop it | | Approval resolved | A decision has been made on the approval request | Approved: the agent continues with the action. Rejected: it drops the action and may look for another approach | Approval is triggered because the action may be risky or affect important files; it is a safety mechanism. To see fewer approvals, talk to an administrator about adjusting the approval mode. Abnormal statuses | Status | Meaning | Causes | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Failed | The agent ran into a problem and could not finish the task | A file is missing or unreadable; a network request failed; a tool errored out; the AI model service had a problem | Read the error for the cause, adjust the request as it suggests, such as giving the right file path, then retry | | Cancelled | The conversation was stopped, by you or by the system | You clicked Stop; the system timed out and cancelled; some other deliberate stop | Start the conversation again, or review the record of what ran before the cancellation | | Stuck session | It stays in one state for a long time with no progress | The network connection dropped; the backend service had a problem; task handling timed out | Wait a few minutes first; if it is genuinely stuck, click Stop; use the reset work state option in settings to clear the abnormal state; if it still does not recover, contact an administrator | Connection status | Status | Meaning | Symptoms and handling | | --- | --- | --- | | Connected | The network connection to the backend service is fine | — | | Disconnected | The network connection to the backend service has dropped | You cannot send new messages, the status display looks wrong, and a "connection lost" notice appears; check your network, refresh the page or restart the app, and wait for the automatic reconnect | Where status indicators appear | Location | What it shows | | --- | --- | | Above the conversation | The overall status of the current session | | Beside a message bubble | The processing status of that message | | In the progress area | Detailed progress of tool execution | | Lower or right part of the chat | The run trace and tool call record: which tools ran, which files were read, what actions were performed | Diagnosis Slow responses: a complex task that needs several steps, a slow AI model service, or high system load all lengthen the response time. Wait rather than resending the same message. Status display looks wrong: wait first to see whether it recovers on its own; if not, use the reset work state option; then refresh the page or restart the app. If it still persists, follow Troubleshooting. Status overview Basic statuses Approval statuses Abnormal statuses Connection status Where status indicators appear Diagnosis

title: Prompts and Personalization
summary: The built-in packs `default-zh` and `default-en`, the segments a pack is made of, switching and effect rules, and how to create a custom pack.
headings: What a pack is made of
text: Prompts and Personalization The built-in packs default-zh and default-en, the segments a pack is made of, switching and effect rules, and how to create a custom pack. A prompt template sets the agent's role and answer style. Two built-in packs ship with wunder — default-zh and default-en — and custom packs can be created in the interface. Prompt templates A template sets four things: The role How to think and answer The working principles and limits How to use tools and skills Switch to another template and the agent's style and emphasis change with it. Built-in template packs | Pack | Language | Fits | | --- | --- | --- | | default-zh | Thinks and answers in Chinese | Chinese-language conversations; the default Chinese assistant style | | default-en | Thinks and answers in English | English-language conversations; the default English assistant style | Pick the pack that matches the language the user mostly works in. A template only sets a default tendency: even with default-zh, asking for English in the conversation is followed. What a pack is made of Each pack is assembled from several segments: | Segment | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Role | Defines who the agent is and what role it plays | | Engineering principles | Defines how it works and thinks | | Tool protocol | Defines how it uses tools | | Skill protocol | Defines how it invokes skills | | Memory | Defines how it uses long-term memory | | Extra notes | Additional instructions | Switching packs Switching steps 1. Go to Settings at the bottom of the left sidebar → Agent 2. Find the prompt template option 3. Choose the pack you want 4. Save When it takes effect New conversations: ones created after the switch use the new template Existing conversations: unchanged, keeping the template from when they were created A conversation fixes its prompt when it is created and then keeps it frozen, so behavior stays consistent and does not shift partway through. An existing conversation's prompt cannot be edited directly: start a new conversation to use the new template, or copy the content you want to keep into a new conversation and continue there. Creating a custom template Creation steps 1. In the template settings page, click New template pack 2. Pick a template to copy as the base; starting from a built-in one works well 3. Edit the content of each segment 4. Save, and it is ready to use Writing each segment Role segment: state the role, such as "coding assistant" or "data analysis expert" Engineering principles: set the answer style, concise or detailed, formal or casual Tool protocol: usually leave it alone Extra notes: put your own specific requirements here Example: a coding assistant template The role segment might read: How templates layer The agent's final prompt is combined from several layers: 1. System template: the global base set by an administrator 2. User template: the pack the user picked 3. Agent settings: extra configuration for that particular agent An upper layer overrides a lower one, and anything missing falls back to the lower layer. Each agent configures its template independently. Writing notes Start from a built-in template, then customize from there Create a separate pack for each scenario if you like State the key requirements clearly and avoid redundancy; longer is not better, and a long or self-contradictory template works against that Do not put contradictory requirements in the same template Review it occasionally and drop entries you no longer need Prompt templates Built-in template packs What a pack is made of Switching packs Switching steps When it takes effect Creating a custom template Creation steps Writing each segment Example: a coding assistant template How templates layer Writing notes

title: System Settings Reference
summary: The six settings categories, configuration layers and effect timing, and a configuration comparison across two deployment forms.
text: System Settings Reference The six settings categories, configuration layers and effect timing, and a configuration comparison across two deployment forms. Settings fall into six categories by responsibility: Basic settings: service address, port, and run mode Security settings: access control and permission boundaries Storage settings: where and how data is stored Tool settings: which tools are available Model settings: AI model selection and parameters Channel settings: external platform access New settings take effect for new sessions immediately; existing sessions do not change and keep the settings from when they were created. The three layers, bottom to top, are system defaults (the bottom layer that any unset value falls back to), per-user settings (override the system defaults and affect only that user), and agent settings (the top layer, affecting only that agent). The order of precedence is agent settings > user settings > system defaults. Basic settings Service address and port For local use, keep the defaults; for a team deployment, set an address the team can reach. Run mode Two values: Pupa local mode (all data stored locally) and Hull mode (multi-user support and centralized management). Pick Pupa local mode for individual use, and Hull mode when you need multi-user collaboration or centralized management. Concurrency limit A cap on how many sessions can be active at once. The default is enough for individual use; for team use, adjust it to the number of users and the available hardware. Security settings API key The credential guarding access to the Bridge and the Hull interfaces. The key should be long enough — over 16 characters, mixing letters, digits, and symbols; do not use a key that is easy to guess, and rotate the key regularly. Path access control Limits the file paths the agent may touch and the commands it may run: Allowed paths: the directories the agent may work in Denied patterns: the file types or paths that are off limits Do not open the whole filesystem: name the working directories the agent may use and block sensitive system directories. External auth key Used to verify external requests when wunder is embedded in another system, or when another system calls into wunder's capabilities. Storage settings Database type SQLite: a lightweight local database, suited to Pupa local mode (default) PostgreSQL: a full-scale database, suited to the Hull multi-user mode Workspace location Where user files and agent artifacts are stored. In Hull mode, make sure the workspace directory is persistent (use NAS or network storage); do not put the workspace in a temporary directory. Vector storage The storage backend used by knowledge-base retrieval, saved alongside the main storage backend: PostgreSQL in Hull mode and SQLite in Pupa local mode. Configure it when you need knowledge-base retrieval. Tool settings Built-in tool switches Controls which built-in tools the agent may use. In sensitive environments, consider turning off command-execution tools and opening only what is actually needed. Browser tools Once enabled, the agent can browse pages and take screenshots. Enable them directly for local use; a Hull deployment may need Docker container support. MCP extension tools External tool services connected over the MCP protocol. Use them for specialized database operations, particular API calls, or third-party services. Model settings Available model list The AI models the agent can choose from. Adding a model means supplying its API key and endpoint Different models have different billing and different strengths Offering several options lets users pick what fits Context limit A cap on the conversation context length. Setting it to the model's maximum is fine; when the limit is reached, the system compresses older content automatically. Channel settings Channel account binding Binds accounts on external platforms such as Feishu and WeCom. Create an app on the platform, obtain its credentials, and fill in the configuration for that channel type. Webhook configuration The receiving address external platforms push messages to. Set up a publicly reachable address and configure the webhook URL on the external platform. Deployment forms | Item | Individual local use (Pupa desktop) | Team collaboration (Hull server) | | --- | --- | --- | | Database | SQLite (default) | PostgreSQL | | Workspace | A local directory | Network storage (persistent) | | Security | Limit sensitive paths reasonably | Configure keys and path limits strictly | | Tools | Open them as needed | Assign permissions by role | Basic settings Service address and port Run mode Concurrency limit Security settings API key Path access control External auth key Storage settings Database type Workspace location Vector storage Tool settings Built-in tool switches Browser tools MCP extension tools Model settings Available model list Context limit Channel settings Channel account binding Webhook configuration Deployment forms

title: Workspace Routing and File Management
summary: Uniqueness and isolation of the cloud directory, how `/wunder/workspace*` is resolved, path conventions, usage statistics, and file management.
text: Workspace Routing and File Management Uniqueness and isolation of the cloud directory, how /wunder/workspace is resolved, path conventions, usage statistics, and file management. Every user has a single cloud directory. Cloud Directory Isolation has one layer only: by user. Each user's files live in their own single cloud directory, partitioned by the server under its data root. | Convention | Meaning | |------|------| | Unique | There is only one workspace directory at any time; opening more threads or subagents never adds another | | Fixed | You cannot add, delete, or replace the directory, and you cannot bind a folder on your machine | | Isolated | Path checks are bounded by the user root; out-of-bounds access is rejected | | Persistent | The workspace is persistent storage and is not cleaned up automatically | Routing Rules Routing for /wunder/workspace: 1. The request carries the signed-in user's identity 2. The server resolves that user's workspace root 3. The entry is located under that root by the relative path in the request The container parameter has been converged: the historical containerid no longer selects a directory, and the server always resolves against the user root. The parameter is still accepted during the transition, but 0 and 1 produce the same result, and the front end no longer offers a container choice. No more per-agent roots: agentid only affects conversation and configuration binding, not directory derivation. Subagents do not get their own directory: a subagent is a temporary work unit created by the main agent and shares the same user directory. Path Conventions The API takes and returns workspace-relative paths, for example docs/notes.md The root directory is written as an empty string Do not pass a machine absolute path, and never show a server absolute path in the front end Invalid or out-of-bounds names are rejected outright rather than silently redirected Workspace versus Temporary Directory | | Workspace | Temporary directory | |--|--------|----------| | Purpose | Long-lived files and task artifacts | Transit for uploads and downloads, and document-conversion intermediates | | Lifecycle | Persistent, never cleaned automatically | May be cleaned periodically | | Paths | Workspace-relative | A separate transit namespace | Keep files you need to keep in the workspace and transit files in the temporary directory. Usage Statistics GET /wunder/workspace/stats returns a bare object whose fields include the file count, directory count, bytes used, whether the walk was truncated, and recently modified files: The walk is bounded; it ends early for very large directories, and a true truncated means the counts are a lower bound A null quotabytes means no quota is configured; the interface then shows only the used amount, with no quota denominator The working-directory overview card on the welcome page and the usage bar at the bottom of the left sidebar share this data File Management Browse: directories load lazily, fetching children only when expanded; large directories are paginated and rows are virtualized Upload: use the toolbar, or drag files onto the file-tree area; uploads are concurrency-limited and can be cancelled or retried Preview and edit: text, images, Office documents, and diagrams each have a preview or online-edit overlay Reference to chat: choose "Reference to chat" in a file row menu to bring the file into the composer; entries in the timeline link back to it Batch and archive: multi-select to delete in bulk or download an archive High-risk operations: deleting or clearing a directory needs a second confirmation; front-end confirmation never replaces server-side authorization Uploads and File Types | Type | Handling | |------|------| | Documents (PDF, Word, Markdown, and so on) | Converted to text automatically for the agent to analyze | | Images (PNG, JPG, and so on) | The agent can view and analyze them directly | | Audio (MP3, WAV, and so on) | Transcribed to text automatically | | Video (MP4, and so on) | Frames are extracted at a set rate for analysis | | Code files | Files in various programming languages, which the agent can read directly | | Other | Stored as-is, and the agent can try to read them | Some files must be processed after upload (document-to-text, audio transcription, and so on), and the send button stays disabled until processing finishes. Cloud Directory Routing Rules Path Conventions Workspace versus Temporary Directory Usage Statistics File Management Uploads and File Types

title: Bridge Panel Guide
summary: What each panel in the four groups manages, plus the throughput-test, simulated-model, and random-simulator conventions.
headings: Round conventions of the random simulator
text: Bridge Panel Guide What each panel in the four groups manages, plus the throughput-test, simulated-model, and random-simulator conventions. The Bridge is reached at its own address: open the Bridge URL in a browser and sign in with an administrator account, and the management panels are available. The exact address is fixed at deployment time; ask whoever deployed the system or check the deployment documentation. Panels are organized into four groups: system, agent, debug, and documentation. The Bridge holds the highest privileges in the system: Only authorized administrators can access it Administrator passwords should be strong Rotate administrator passwords regularly Confirm the scope of impact before acting Keep records of important actions | I want to… | Go to this panel | |---------|------------| | Add a user | User management | | Grant a user quota | User management → open the user → Settings | | See how the system is running | Internal status | | Adjust system configuration | System settings | | Add a new model | Model configuration | | View active sessions | Thread management or Internal status | | Handle a stuck thread | Thread management → cancel | | Test system performance | Performance testing or Throughput testing | | Look up how to use something | User guide | System group Internal status Shows how the system is running: Active sessions System load State of key components System settings Global parameters: Service address and port Security settings Storage settings Tool switches Changing a system setting: 1. System settings → find the relevant option 2. Change the value 3. Save (usually takes effect immediately) 4. Confirm the effect in Internal status Organization management Manages the organizational structure: Create and manage organizations Organization hierarchy Organization members User management Manages user accounts: View the user list Create users Edit user details Manage quota accounts (grant, deduct, set balance) The quota actions inside a user's settings: Set the balance directly: overwrites the current balance, which is useful for correcting the recorded figure Grant quota: increases the balance and records the cumulative amount received Deduct quota: reduces the balance and records the cumulative amount consumed Administrator accounts are not subject to balance limits The online status in the user list is split by client: Beehive (web), Pupa (desktop), and Helm (command line). Adding a new user: 1. User management → create user 2. Set the username, password, and organization 3. Grant quota as needed 4. The user can now log in and start working Agent group Model configuration Manages the AI models available: Add a model by filling in its API key and endpoint Configure model parameters Set the default model Thread management Views and manages active threads: Thread status Force-cancelling a thread Viewing thread logs Handling an abnormal session: 1. Thread management → look at the abnormal thread 2. Check the thread logs and status 3. To stop it, click cancel 4. Review the related logs to locate the problem Preset agents There can be several preset agent templates, and each user is bound one-to-one to one of them. Create, edit, and delete presets Configure a preset's tools, model, prompts, and the fields the user may customize View bound users and adjust bindings in bulk (bind, rebind, unbind); unbinding requires naming a new preset Apply preset-managed system configuration to bound users' instances, with a dry run that previews the affected users; user-created MCP, skills, and knowledge-base selection states are preserved Tool management Manages the tools available: View the built-in tool list Configure external MCP tools Set tool permissions System prompts Manages the global prompt templates: View and edit system templates Switch the default template pack Create new packs Debug group Throughput testing Test parameters: a model, a concurrency list, an input length, and an output length. Each run tests one concurrency level from the list in order and fires that many requests at once. The default concurrency list is 1,2,4,8, the default input is 8.2k tokens, and the default output is 128 tokens; the usual presets are kept, and you can also type any integer within range. Readings: token counts are shown as k from 1,000 and as m from 100,000; history snapshots show the input usage actually measured by the API; the right side shows the aggregated input and output, the first-token latency, the generation speed, and the total time; the history curve plots concurrency on the horizontal axis and shows both overall and per-request speeds. Engines that support it receive a fixed-length output parameter; other endpoints may finish early, and the actual usage and the reason for ending are kept in the details. Tests create no sessions or thread logs and keep only the last 50 performance summaries. The details and curves separate overall prefill and generation speed, per-prefill speed, and per-generation speed; speeds are shown as k tok/s from 1,000 and as m tok/s from 100,000. Selecting history entries compares performance curves by concurrency: the vertical axis uses concurrency 1 as the 0% baseline and shows relative change, hovering reveals the measured speed, and you can reuse a configuration or export the selected data. For virtual models, model configuration offers fast, medium, and slow profiles, defaulting to fast: prefill at 2000 / 500 / 100 tokens/s and reasoning plus generation at 200 / 50 / 10 tokens/s. Random replies and throughput simulations both reason before generating content, and log replay uses the recorded reasoning within the configured capability and budget. Throughput tests default to reasoning equal to one quarter of the total output and can be tuned with the reasoning switch and budget; simulated records are tagged and grouped separately by profile. Simulated model capabilities With a virtual model selected in model configuration, you can set the maximum context, maximum output, vision, hearing, reasoning, and tool capabilities. Context and output left empty default to 128k and 4k. When the input (including tool definitions) plus the output budget exceeds the window, a context-overflow is reported. Turning off vision or hearing makes the corresponding media requests fail. Images and audio can each carry a per-item token count; this only simulates usage and time and does not recognize content. Replay follows the tool-calling mode: functioncall uses the native tool channel, toolcall uses the text protocol, and freeformcall falls back to native or text depending on the API mode. Tool names and arguments come straight from the log, so nothing has to be filled in by hand; tool execution still follows permissions and approvals, and replay continues to the next model round once results come back. Running out of log entries raises an error rather than repeating old calls. Synthetic replies do not initiate tools. An over-long output is marked as a length termination, incomplete tool arguments are not executed, and the reasoning capability and budget also apply to throughput tests. Round conventions of the random simulator With no replay log available, the random simulator follows conventions carried by the human input of the current turn. They behave identically in every form (蛹, 蜂巢, 舵机): Rounds: the first number in the input sets the model rounds for this turn and may carry an s / 轮 / 次 suffix (12, 12轮, 1s all read as 12 or 1). The value is capped at 2000 and anything below 1 counts as 1. Only the human input of the current turn is read — never history, so context compaction cannot change the plan mid-turn. Spawning a subagent: an input containing subagent, the shorthand s / sub, 子智能体 / 子代理, or a number followed directly by s (1s) makes the first model round emit a real subagent dispatch (spawn or batchspawn). Such turns span at least two rounds — one to dispatch, one to close — so 1s still spawns the child before answering. Middle rounds pick read-only tools from the request's tool list and issue harmless calls; the last round outputs the summary. The plan is derived deterministically from (session, user round), so cancel-and-resume stays consistent. Performance testing Tests response performance: Single-request latency measurement Performance sampling Capability evaluation Evaluates an agent's capability level: Task-completion quality assessment Capability regression tests Debug panel Live debugging tools: Real-time request tracing Tool-call logs Error investigation LSP Language service protocol debugging: Code intelligence service status LSP configuration validation Documentation group User guide This is the documentation site you are reading now: Getting started Concepts Operating references Troubleshooting Interface reference Lists interface information: Endpoint addresses Field descriptions Usage examples System group Internal status System settings Organization management User management Agent group Model configuration Thread management Preset agents Tool management System prompts Debug group Throughput testing Simulated model capabilities Round conventions of the random simulator Performance testing Capability evaluation Debug panel LSP Documentation group User guide Interface reference

title: WeChat iLink Channel
summary: How `weixin` compares with the legacy WeChat channels, QR-code sign-in, required and optional configuration, media and inbound troubleshooting, and migration steps.
text: WeChat iLink Channel How weixin compares with the legacy WeChat channels, QR-code sign-in, required and optional configuration, media and inbound troubleshooting, and migration steps. weixin is an independent channel; it is not the same set of parameters as wechat or wechatmp. Pick the channel by scenario before integrating. Channel Selection | Scenario | Choose | | --- | --- | | Enterprise WeChat app callback | wechat (legacy) | | WeChat Official Account callback | wechatmp (legacy) | | WeChat capability over the iLink protocol | weixin (new) | The main differences between new and old: Inbound: weixin pulls updates by long polling; the legacy version uses Webhook callbacks. Reply requirement: a weixin reply must carry the context identifier of the current session; the legacy version does not depend on it. Login: weixin scans a QR code to obtain the bot token; the legacy version uses traditional enterprise / Official Account parameters. Media: weixin goes through a CDN and handles encryption and decryption itself; the legacy version goes through the platform's native interface.
