Status: new integrations use weixin; the legacy version is in maintenance / compatibility mode for existing deployments. QR-Code Sign-In After choosing weixin in the channel settings: 1. Click "Generate QR code"; 2. Scan it with WeChat; 3. Click "Wait for confirmation"; 4. The system fills in the bot token, bot ID, user ID, and interface address automatically; 5. Save the account configuration. After the auto-fill you must save, or long polling does not actually take effect. The QR code has a validity period and must be regenerated once it expires. Settings and Troubleshooting Three required fields: interface address, bot token, and bot ID; then turn on the long-connection switch. Optional enhancements: CDN address, bot type, allowed caller range, polling and interface timeouts, backoff after consecutive failures, and route tag. Media-link troubleshooting order: whether media is enabled, whether the CDN address is reachable, whether the decryption key is correct, and whether the attachment exceeds the size limit. A reply reporting "missing session context identifier" means the reply did not receive the context identifier from the previous inbound message. Confirm the reply goes through the same session and that the inbound message preserved it. Not receiving messages for a long time: check in order whether the account is active, whether the long connection is on, whether the token and bot ID are valid, and whether the session has expired in the Bridge runtime view. Sessions expiring frequently: usually the login state is lost; scan again for a new token and save. Migration Steps 1. Run in parallel first: keep the old channel and let new traffic prefer weixin; 2. Switch over by account, in batches; 3. Watch inbound success rate, outbound success rate, first-packet latency, and the failure ranking; 4. Once stable, mark the old channel as maintenance mode. Channel Selection QR-Code Sign-In Settings and Troubleshooting Migration Steps

title: Chat WebSocket
summary: The handshake flow, client message types, server returns, and reconnect behavior of `/wunder/chat/ws`.
text: Chat WebSocket The handshake flow, client message types, server returns, and reconnect behavior of /wunder/chat/ws. /wunder/chat/ws is both the event-push channel and the control channel for a session: starting an execution, resuming after a disconnect, watching, canceling, and returning approvals all happen on the same connection. Chat and desktop real-time sessions both use it, and there is no SSE fallback. Use Cases Chat workbenches and desktop sessions; Starting, resuming, watching, and canceling an execution on the same connection; Long-lived connection keepalive and consistent real-time state. Handshake Flow 1. Create a session and take its ID. 2. Open the WebSocket connection. 3. Send the connect handshake. 4. Receive ready. 5. Send start to begin an execution. 6. Keep consuming event until this round's terminal state, turnterminal. Handshake example: Starting an execution: Message Types Client to server: | kind | Effect | | --- | --- | | connect | Handshake and protocol negotiation | | start | Begin an execution | | resume | Catch up on events missed after a disconnect | | watch | Observe a session without driving it | | cancel | Cancel the current execution | | approval | Return an approval decision | | ping | Keepalive | The server mainly returns ready, event, error, and pong. Settings and Limits Event categories to consume: queued, approval resolved, error, and end of turn. turnterminal is the terminal signal for a single execution round and works as the frontend's convergence condition. start must explicitly carry the session ID. The body text uses content, not /wunder's question. resume (catching up on events) and watch (observing the runtime state) are two different actions. Approvals on this connection only handle approval items that come from the WebSocket. Disconnect and Reconnect Do not fall back to SSE. Reconnect to /wunder/chat/ws, then send as the situation requires: resume: carry the position of the last handled event to fill in the events missed during the disconnect. watch: observe the current session's runtime state again. Use Cases Handshake Flow Message Types Settings and Limits Disconnect and Reconnect

title: MCP Endpoint
summary: The address and transport of the MCP service wunder exposes, the built-in `excute` and `doc2md` tools, and how to configure an external MCP service.
text: MCP Endpoint The address and transport of the MCP service wunder exposes, the built-in excute and doc2md tools, and how to configure an external MCP service. wunder can expose itself as an MCP service and act as an MCP client to connect to external services. The two directions have separate entry points and configurations. Two Directions | Direction | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Expose | Let external systems call wunder's capabilities over MCP | | Connect external | Bring external capabilities in for the model to use | Exposing wunder The outward entry is a single address, served over Streamable HTTP. The order in which it comes together: 1. The external system connects to that address following the MCP protocol; 2. wunder negotiates the protocol version automatically; when it interoperates with an older service it settles on a version both sides support, so the initialization step does not have to be written by hand; 3. Call the specific tools. Two tools are built in for external callers: excute (execute) and doc2md (document to Markdown). The tool name is literally excute; call it by exactly that name. Connecting an External Service Declare the MCP service you want to connect in the configuration — give it a name, an address, and a transport — then switch it on. Once enabled, wunder treats it as a callable service. External services also use Streamable HTTP; when a service is written in Python, it negotiates according to the Python side's protocol version and may not carry every latest capability. A typical example is the external service often mentioned in the documentation, which usually hosts tools such as database query, database export, and knowledge-base query. Settings and Limits Integration order: declare the service in the configuration → confirm in Bridge that the tool list can be fetched → then expose it to the model. Bridge has MCP configuration and debugging entries where you can refresh the tool list and call remote tools directly to verify them. MCP tools are not a side channel: they are aggregated with built-in tools, A2A tools, skills, knowledge-base tools, and self-built tools into one tool view. To the model, MCP is just part of the tool catalog. Two Directions Exposing wunder Connecting an External Service Settings and Limits
